If only the moose had brought a skateboard with him to the skate park. All this excitement could have been avoided.

title: Mamdani dined at NYC restaurant linked to anti-Israel menu after being booed at Oct 7 vigil: report
excerpt:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani doubled down on his October 7 statement accusing Israel of carrying out a "genocide" in Gaza on Thursday.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani dined Wednesday at a Pa...
body_text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani doubled down on his October 7 statement accusing Israel of carrying out a "genocide" in Gaza on Thursday.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani dined Wednesday at a Palestinian restaurant whose sister location faced intense criticism in 2023 over menu language that critics called anti-Semitic.

Mamdani ate at Ayat Hinds Hall on the Upper West Side. The restaurant chain, which also operates a location in Brooklyn, drew sharp pushback for featuring a section on its menu titled "From the River to the Sea."

The Anti-Defamation League defines the phrase as an implicit call for the eradication of Israel.

MAMDANI SAYS IT WAS 'STRANGE' GETTING CALLED OUT BY NETANYAHU AFTER CALLING FOR HIS ARREST

A group of anti-Israel protesters targeted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, calling him a "traitor." (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)

The menu’s front page reads: "Down with the occupation," in English, Arabic, and Hebrew, The Times of Israel reported.

"Resilience," "Freedom," and "Save our children" are pictured in bold letters. The menu also includes a map that refers to the the West Bank, Gaza, Jerusalem and Israel as Palestine.

Following the 2023 controversy, critics accused the restaurant of being "opening genocidal" toward Jews.

Owner Abdul Elenani pushed back against accusations of antisemitism, noting the phrase had been on the menu months prior to Hamas's Oct. 7 attack on Israel.

SCHUMER, JEFFRIES DODGE MAMDANI CONTROVERSY AS FELLOW NEW YORK DEM UNLOADS

NYC Mayor Zorhan Mamdani ate at Ayat Hinds Hall, a Middle Eastern restaurant on the Upper West Side on Wednesday, on the third anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks on Israel by Hamas. The restaurant came under fire in 2023 after a menu at one of its locations had a section titled: "From the River to the Sea," a slogan frequently used by anti-Israel protesters. (Getty Images; Google Maps)

Elenani stated that he supports a two-state solution and condemns violence on both sides, according to the New York Post. In 2024, he organized a free Shabbat dinner for hundreds of guests, the Times report states.

Mamdani’s dinner came shortly after he faced backlash from pro-Palestinian demonstrators during a vigil marking the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 attacks.

Demonstrators booed the mayor — a frequent critic of Israel's military campaign in Gaza — and accused him of being a "traitor" who enables genocide.

"Zohran, what do you say? How many kids did you kill today?" protesters shouted, according to media reports. "700,000 dead. Mamdani, your hands are red!"

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Mamdani stood by his previous statements characterizing Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide while calling for universal empathy.

"I believe that there must be room to mourn every single life," Mamdani said. "There must be room to mourn the lives of the more than 1,100 that Hamas killed three years ago; there must be room to mourn the 74,000 Palestinians that the Israeli government has killed since."

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Polls close in Holborn and St Pancras byelection as Labour hopes to retain seat
excerpt:
Contest seen as test of Andy Burnham’s ability to unite Labour voters amid threat from Green party’s Zack Polanski

Polls have closed in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, a contest seen as a test...
body_text:
Contest seen as test of Andy Burnham’s ability to unite Labour voters amid threat from Green party’s Zack Polanski

Polls have closed in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, a contest seen as a test of whether Andy Burnham can unite Labour’s voters or whether Zack Polanski can peel off support from the party’s progressive flank.

Labour is seeking to retain Keir Starmer’s former north London seat, where he won a majority of more than 11,000 votes in the 2024 general election.

The byelection is seen as a measure of the political landscape under Burnham, almost three months into his premiership.

It is a significant first electoral test for Burnham, who succeeded Starmer in July, as part of a wider battle for younger leftwing voters who became disillusioned with the party under Starmer’s leadership over issues such as housing, the climate crisis and the war in Gaza.

Polanski has sought to run an energetic campaign involving thousands of activists, leaving the Green party conference early after his speech in an attempt to prove he and the Greens are a serious rival to Labour, despite the latest polling.

The Greens are hoping to reproduce their byelection victory in Gorton and Denton in February where they overturned a Labour majority.

However, the political landscape has shifted since then. Shortly after their byelection win in Greater Manchester, YouGov polling put the Greens on 21%, a few points ahead of Labour.

But the latest YouGov survey put the Greens 16 points behind Burnham’s Labour, which was on 27%. The poll came as Burnham proposed a more ambitious pitch to progressives at his first Labour conference as prime minister.

Holborn and St Pancras has a large number of students, younger voters and renters, with almost half of residents aged between 18 and 34, while about 45% were born overseas.

Polanski has argued that electing him would increase pressure on Labour to deliver more radical policies, including stronger rent controls, greater action on the climate crisis and public ownership of Thames Water.

But the leader of the Greens has faced questions about his own authority and was accused of being unable to articulate his thoughts on motions that became policies at his party’s conference.

In an interview with the Guardian last Friday, Polanski described the contest as “probably 50/50” and that it was “really on a knife-edge” while also insisting his leadership did not depend on victory.

Asked whether losing the byelection would undermine his position, Polanski said: “It doesn’t depend on it whatsoever.”

Senior Green figures privately fear a defeat could severely damage his reputation amid concerns the party’s increase in members has not translated into an advantage in campaigning.

Labour has fielded Sagal Abdi-Wali, the 42-year-old leader of Camden council who arrived in Britain as a child refugee after her family fled civil war in Somalia.

She has emphasised her longstanding connections to the area, presenting herself as locally rooted, and with experience of community work, homelessness and housing policy.

The closing days of the byelection campaign were overshadowed by a row within the Green party after members voted at their conference to adopt a policy equating Zionism with racism, which passed by 1,022 votes to 813 despite opposition from four of the party’s five MPs.

Polanski, who is Jewish, left the conference early to campaign in north London and did not participate in the vote.

The byelection result may provide some insight into whether Burnham’s recovery in national support is translating into Labour’s inner-city strongholds, and into whether the Greens can continue to attract younger and progressive voters.

It will also offer a test of Polanski’s argument that the Greens can put pressure on the government from the left, even as Labour seeks to reclaim voters it lost under Starmer.

Polls closed at 10pm on Thursday and the result is likely to be announced between 2:30am and 4am on Friday.

title: Haverford professor charged over alleged ‘heinous’ antisemitic online attacks, barred from campus
excerpt:
Haverford College professor Guangtian Ha was arrested and charged with federal cyberstalking after allegedly sending antisemitic threats to a Jewish colleague. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

A Haverford ...
body_text:
Haverford College professor Guangtian Ha was arrested and charged with federal cyberstalking after allegedly sending antisemitic threats to a Jewish colleague. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

A Haverford College professor was arrested Tuesday and charged with federal cyberstalking after allegedly sending dozens of antisemitic threats to a colleague in Pennsylvania, prompting the college to bar him from campus, more than two years after Jewish students accused the same professor of making threatening statements about supporters of Israel in a separate lawsuit against the school.

Haverford College President Wendy Raymond addressed the arrest of religion professor Guangtian Ha in a statement provided to Fox News Digital by a college spokesperson.

"I am heartbroken and furious at the possibility that an individual within our community would seek to inflict such pain on another," Raymond said. "This disturbing news is made even more harmful for many given its proximity to both the Jewish High Holidays and the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks."

Haverford College President Wendy Raymond condemned the alleged antisemitic harassment and confirmed that Ha had been placed on administrative leave and barred from campus. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

ISRAELI MEDICS TRAIN US SYNAGOGUES HOW TO RESPOND TO ATTACKS, AS HIGH HOLIDAYS APPROACH

According to a federal indictment, Ha allegedly used at least four anonymous X accounts to send approximately 50 threatening messages to a Jewish colleague between October 2025 and May 2026.

Prosecutors alleged that Ha posted the colleague's home address, referenced the colleague's children and made statements invoking the Holocaust. The colleague's spouse and three children temporarily left their home twice because of the threats, according to The Philadelphia Inquirer.

The arrest follows earlier allegations against Ha that were included in a 2024 antisemitism lawsuit against Haverford College. In a January 2025 amended complaint, Jewish students accused Ha of publishing hostile social media posts about supporters of Israel, including one in which he allegedly said he knew their identities.

The complaint reproduced a statement attributed to Ha targeting people within his Haverford community who remained silent about, or supported, what he characterized as genocide.

"I will never forgive them," Ha said, according to the complaint. "I know their names and I know their faces. Never forgive. No reconciliation."

Ha allegedly used at least four anonymous X accounts to send approximately 50 threatening messages to a Jewish colleague between October 2025 and May 2026. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

FBI NABS 7 FOR ALLEGED 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE' TO PRESSURE UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN, BUSINESSES OVER ISRAEL TIES

The plaintiffs alleged that Ha's remarks were threatening and that college administrators had been informed of his posts by September 2024. They further alleged that Haverford had taken no effective action against him at the time of the January 2025 filing.

The earlier lawsuit did not establish that Ha engaged in unlawful conduct, and the allegations in that case are distinct from the federal cyberstalking charge.

Raymond said the college had placed Ha, who was already on sabbatical and not teaching during the academic year, on administrative leave pending the criminal proceedings over the "heinous online attacks."

"I am deeply distressed by these allegations and want to state in the plainest of terms that any form of harassment or discrimination based on identity is unacceptable, antithetical to our values, and has no place at Haverford," Raymond said.

Ha had previously been named in a 2024 antisemitism lawsuit against Haverford College, which alleged that he posted threatening statements about supporters of Israel before his arrest. (Getty Images)

WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM

The arrest came just two months after Haverford settled the lawsuit brought by Jewish members of its community over allegations that administrators failed to adequately address antisemitic harassment following Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attacks against Israel.

As part of the August settlement, the college committed to annual antisemitism awareness training, revisions to campus policies and the creation of a committee to address antisemitism. A federal judge had previously dismissed the plaintiffs' Title VI discrimination claim while allowing a breach-of-contract claim to proceed.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Raymond also acknowledged the involvement of federal and local authorities in investigating the allegations against Ha.

"I also want to thank the FBI, Haverford Township Police Department, and Campus Safety for aiding in the investigation," Raymond said.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

You can send news tips to cj.womack@fox.com and follow CJ on Twitter.

title: Trump gives top US science awards to Elon Musk and other tech executives
excerpt: United States President Donald Trump has awarded the country’s most prestigious honours in science and engineering to executives from top technology firms including SpaceX, Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvi...
body_text:
United States President Donald Trump has awarded the country’s most prestigious honours in science and engineering to executives from top technology firms including SpaceX, Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvidia.

On Thursday, Trump presented the National Medal of Science to billionaire SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Lisa Su of the semiconductor firm AMD.

Two more recipients received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation: Michael Dell of Dell Technologies and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.

At the award ceremony, Trump credited the honourees with “helping pioneer an incredible future for America”.

“Because of these people here, we will always be on top. No one else can compete with us,” Trump said.

Five of the six people receiving medals on Thursday were born outside the US. Four are among the 10 wealthiest people in the world, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

The award ceremony took place hours after the Trump administration announced it was suspending Microsoft and other top tech companies from using the H-1B visa system, which allows companies to hire skilled foreign workers and put them on a path towards permanent residency in the US.

The suspension, officials said, was due to the companies allegedly using the system in a fraudulent manner.

The medal ceremony was the latest example of what critics see as an increasingly close relationship between Silicon Valley tech executives and the second Trump administration.

Powerful companies like Amazon, Meta and Nvidia contributed money to Trump’s second inauguration, and several high-profile industry leaders attended his swearing-in, including Musk and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

Trump, for his part, has pledged to slash regulations and position the US “as the world leader in artificial intelligence”.

He has also touted self-regulation in the AI industry amid concerns about the safety of the technology.

Several of the tech entrepreneurs honoured on Thursday have forged close ties to the White House, through political and business dealings.

The South Africa-born Musk, for example, was the largest contributor to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign and has been a supporter of right-wing causes around the world, which he amplifies on his social media platform, X.

He briefly served as a special adviser to the president during the first months of Trump’s second term, helping to lead the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and its efforts to downsize the federal government.

Around the time he left DOGE, however, Musk and Trump had a public falling-out over the president’s tax-and-spending plans.

The two have since reconciled. On Thursday, Trump hailed Musk as “our modern-day Thomas Edison” and an “industrial titan”, citing his work with the aerospace company SpaceX and the carmaker Tesla.

“Few Americans in history have done more to advance America’s national interest than Elon in one field after another,” Trump said.

Another honouree, Dell, has been a financial backer of the president’s efforts to launch Trump Accounts, a scheme to enrol American children born during Trump’s second term into government-backed investment accounts.

Dell and his wife Susan Dell committed $6.25bn to the programme last year.

Separately, the White House entered into a deal in August for the US government to take a 15 percent cut of any AI chip sales that Nvidia and AMD make with China.

Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder, later invested in the struggling US tech firm Intel. He is reported to be among the donors financing Trump’s plans for a new White House ballroom.

The National Medal of Science was first awarded in 1963 to Theodore von Karman, a pioneer in aerospace engineering who fled anti-Semitism in Europe during World War II.

He went on to help found the Jet Propulsion Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology.

Nominations for the award are solicited by the National Science Foundation, and the recipients are ultimately selected by a committee appointed by the president.

title: Israel promotes film that mimics NAZA documentary
excerpt:
Embassies post links to hastily produced online film echoing style of real Guardian documentary about mass killings of Gaza civilians

The Israeli government is promoting an online film project that m...
body_text:
Embassies post links to hastily produced online film echoing style of real Guardian documentary about mass killings of Gaza civilians

The Israeli government is promoting an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, the award-winning documentary that details Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, in an attempt to counter the real film’s findings.

The real documentary, directed by Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and produced by the Guardian, is in cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries.

The Israeli government has denounced the film and announced plans to strip Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, accusing them of treason.

In recent days, Israeli embassies have been promoting a link to a hastily produced online film entitled NAZA: The Real Story. Mimicking some of the style of the real documentary, including the use of anonymised interviews shot on rooftops in Tel Aviv, it is hosted on a website called nazadocumentary.com.

Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made the new documentary, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians, toward claims that it is the “most moral army in the world”.

Another film-maker listed on the website for NAZA: The Real Story is Roi Danino, a candidate for the rightwing Israel First party.

The website domain was registered on 16 September, six days after NAZA’s premiere at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize after receiving the longest ovation in the festival’s history.

Initially, the website falsely presented itself as a promotional page for NAZA itself, naming Abraham and Szor as the directors, and listing film festivals where the documentary was due to be screened.

“Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film reveals in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of terrorists in Gaza,” it said, distorting the film’s official synopsis by removing the reference to the deaths of Palestinian civilians.

That wording was removed from recent updates of the website, once the video for NAZA: The Real Story had been added to the page.

It now appears as a platform for the rival film, with a counter that implausibly suggests the short film has been watched more than 42m times. (The film’s official YouTube page is listed as having just 30,000 views.)

According to a technical analysis, the discrepancy suggested the viewer counter could have been driven by requests made to the website, by humans or bots, rather than the number of people who actually watched the video. When asked about the source of the 42m claim, Averbuch said he did not know and referred the questions to his tech team.

The Israeli military has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023, in a military campaign that a United Nations commission has described as genocide.

The 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders in the original film NAZA detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.

The Israeli embassy to the US, which shared the new documentary on its social media, said the ministry of foreign affairs was not involved in producing the film, and that it had intended only to “amplify the message of its creators and expose wider audiences to arguments challenging and dismantling the blood libels and false allegations”.

The Israeli government said on Thursday that it was awarding the filmmakers with a certificate of appreciation “for their contribution to Israeli public diplomacy”, claiming the production had garnered tens of millions of views.

A Guardian spokesperson said: “We are aware that the Israeli government has been promoting a film hosted on a website that initially – and falsely – claimed it was Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary.

“This was a brazen attempt to mislead audiences and distract from the urgent questions raised by NAZA.”

As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.

Averbuch is the founder of an organisation which says it conducts “advocacy warfare”, including through the publication of scripts to help influencers criticise Abraham and Szor’s critically acclaimed previous film, No Other Land, which documents the destruction of the Palestinian village Masafer Yatta. The two Palestinian co-directors of No Other Land, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, have been harassed or detained by the Israeli military since the film won an Oscar in 2025.

Israeli government officials have scrambled to discredit NAZA’s content, while far-right activists have threatened to hunt down the directors.

The Israel Defense Forces’ chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has said they will use “every tool at our disposal” against the film, while the military has issued a 10-page response to the film, which was based on interviews with more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.

Within a week of NAZA’s premiere, Israel’s ministry of culture had announced a formal investigation into the documentary, calling for Abraham and Szor to be stripped of their citizenship.

Demonstrators gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents, demanding that the she face the death penalty, and a mural depicting the film-makers through the sights of a gun appeared in the Israeli city of Ashdod.

On Monday, the far-right Israeli activist Mordechai David announced he was fundraising in order to establish a team that would “chase” Abraham. “We’ll find him,” David said in a video posted to Instagram.

Szor and Abraham addressed the backlash to their documentary at a Q&A after its New York premiere. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”

title: What would make your life easier? Martin Lewis asks public for ‘small ideas’ to improve UK
excerpt:
Finance expert launches Small Ideas Initiative to gather ‘practical, low-cost’ ideas to put before cross-party panel

Every day, people run into what the finance expert Martin Lewis calls “the life-po...
body_text:
Finance expert launches Small Ideas Initiative to gather ‘practical, low-cost’ ideas to put before cross-party panel

Every day, people run into what the finance expert Martin Lewis calls “the life-potholes of unintended consequences” – clunky systems and poorly conceived rules that make things harder than they should be. His latest project, the Small Ideas Initiative, will attempt to address that, with a cross-party panel of politicians and policymakers crowdsourcing ideas for everyday fixes to take to government.

The ideas could cover anything, from health and schools to policing, tech and money. Lewis is encouraging people to submit ideas for “practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK” before 12 November.

“If we can fix some of those frustration points, we can make people’s lives easier, save time and help everyone get on with work or the things they enjoy,” said Lewis.

“There’s just a sense that there’s so many little things to fix,”said Polly Mackenzie, who worked with Lewis to come up with the idea. Mackenzie, who was director of policy to Nick Clegg during his deputy premiership, says the initiative could be an avenue to regaining trust in public institutions.

“I think this is about rebuilding confidence in the idea that government can sort stuff out, rather than rebuilding confidence on any one political party having the right ideas,” she said.

Mackenzie will sit on the panel, which will choose about 50 ideas to take to the government, councils and regulators. Alongside Lewis, the initiative is run by the innovation charity Nesta and public participation charity Involve.

The Reform MP Danny Kruger, the former Conservative MP Penny Mordaunt, and the Labour mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin, are among those sitting on the panel alongside Mackenzie. She said the group had “a real interest and capability in getting involved and sweating the small stuff”.

The ideas they are looking for will be “no-brainers” that are not party-political and would be easy fixes. Mackenzie said a good example was when she and Lewis first set up the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute and discovered through a survey that GPs had been charging to fill out debt and mental health evidence forms.

“People in debt crisis were having to pay 80, 100, 150 quid to get forbearance for their debts, which is just wrong-headed,” she said. In 2019, two years after the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute started its campaign, the law changed.

Before the initiative’s launch, people in north London shared the policies they would consider submitting. Clare, a railway worker, suggested the government should increase rubbish collections during heatwaves, saying her bins had been “a buffet for flies” this summer. Mark, who works on a market stall, said he would ask the government to put more bins in and around train stations: “There are no bins. I know it’s for security reasons, but I think they could find a way,” he said.

Kwajo Tweneboa, a social housing campaigner who will also sit on the deciding panel, said relatively small changes could make a “massive difference”.

“One small change I’d like to see is housing providers aiming to fix repairs properly the first time, rather than repeatedly applying plaster fixes that don’t address the underlying problem and just prolong the misery for tenants,” he says. “I’ve seen how something that should be a straightforward repair can drag on for months, with residents having to repeatedly chase their landlord while the problem gets worse.”

He added: “It’s about listening to those everyday experiences and turning simple, practical ideas into policy that can make a tangible difference to people’s lives.”

title: Marco Rubio brushes off questions about Kimberly Guilfoyle pressing donor to pay credit card
excerpt:
US ambassador to Greece allegedly asked Trump donor to pay $100,000 American Express bill

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, brushed off reporters’ questions about recent reports that Kimberly G...
body_text:
US ambassador to Greece allegedly asked Trump donor to pay $100,000 American Express bill

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, brushed off reporters’ questions about recent reports that Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece and Trump family ally, used her position to advance personal interests.

Rubio refused to respond to the latest allegations against Guilfoyle, raised in a Wall Street Journal report, claiming she asked a Trump donor to pay her $100,000 American Express bill in exchange for access to the administration, before her US senate confirmation hearing.

“You guys somehow walk around thinking that because some source told you something, and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel, it’s not the gospel for me,” Rubio told reporters while visiting Athens on Wednesday.

Rubio refused to answer questions regarding Guilfoyle’s reported conduct, the second report of its kind, instead saying “our embassy here is doing a great job” and “our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here”.

The top Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees have asked Rubio to open an investigation into Guilfoyle’s conduct as an ambassador, though it’s unclear whether this has happened.

A lawyer for Guilfoyle told the newspaper that she was “owed a balance” for travel and speaking at events before her nomination. Deters told the Wall Street Journal that he did not owe Guilfoyle any balance.

Concerns about Guilfoyle’s conduct were first raised in September when the Wall Street Journal reported she had used her position to invite Greek lobbyists to sit in on official diplomatic meetings and promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company.

Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee sent a letter to Rubio on Tuesday, asking him to look into the allegations against Guilfoyle.

“Such actions do not serve US credibility overseas and risk undermining US diplomacy,” Shaheen wrote. “In advance of your upcoming travel to Greece, I request an immediate review of Ambassador Guilfoyle’s actions and a clarification of what steps have and will be taken to avoid undue influence and even the appearance of a conflict of interest.”

Separately, Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, sent a letter to Rubio in September, requesting more information about Guilfoyle’s conduct, her relationship with the Greek construction and energy company and her relationship with the lobbyist.

“If these reports are accurate, Ambassador Guilfoyle is unfit to represent the United States abroad and should be removed from her position,” Meeks wrote.

Guilfoyle, 57, was once a member of the Trump family’s inner circle, having been engaged to Donald Trump Jr, the US president’s eldest son, for roughly three years. The couple ended their engagement in 2024, and shortly after taking office, Donald Trump nominated Guilfoyle to be ambassador to Greece.

But now further allegations accuse Guilfoyle of promising a Trump donor, Eric Deters, access to the Trump administration in exchange for a $100,000 payment to American Express.

Deters shared messages exchanged between himself and Guilfoyle with the Wall Street Journal in which she reportedly pleaded: “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.”

Deters said Guilfoyle has promised himshe would “be your Trump ride or die, forever and ever” if he made the American Express balance. Deters said he never made the payment.

A lawyer for Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of messages Deters shared with the Wall Street Journal.

It’s unclear whether Shaheen or Meeks will ask Rubio for further information about the latest report. The Guardian has asked Meeks and Shaheen for comment.

title: Microsoft suspended from applying for green cards for H-1B workers, JD Vance says
excerpt:
Vice-president also says Adobe is barred from visa program that allows high-skilled workers to apply for US residency

Microsoft is suspended from applying for permanent residency for workers employed...
body_text:
Vice-president also says Adobe is barred from visa program that allows high-skilled workers to apply for US residency

Microsoft is suspended from applying for permanent residency for workers employed through a US visa program for high-skilled workers, JD Vance announced on Thursday.

The US vice-president accused the tech company of abusing the H-1B system, which allows those on the visa to work while they apply and are in process for a green card.

“Our message to Microsoft is, you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said at a press conference announcing the suspension. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”

Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The US labor department also said Adobe had been similarly suspended.

“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” said Keith Sonderling, the US labor secretary, in a statement.

Microsoft applied for an H-1B visa for nearly 3,700 workers in 2026, making it the fifth largest employer of workers on the visa. Tech companies are the biggest employers of H-1B workers across the industry. Amazon topped the list with more than 9,300 petitions this year. Sonderling said since 2009, Microsoft and Adobe had received about 230,000 approvals for H-1B visas and 100,000 “permanent labor certifications”, a step towards an employment-based green card.

“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one-and-a-half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said.

The Trump administration has set its sights on the H-1B program for some time, arguing that it is rife with abuse. Vance said that on average, workers hired through the H-1B program are making $20,000 less than US workers in the same position.

“So I’m sure that everybody here understands the game that is being played,” Vance said. “You bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers and, if you’re a corporation, you make a ton of money by under cutting the wages of American workers, replacing them with people who, frankly, shouldn’t be in the United States of America to begin with.”

Immigration advocacy groups have long called for reforms for the H-1B program, though for different reasons. Those in the program are often beholden to their employer because their visas are tied to the company that applied for them, making it difficult to switch jobs if things aren’t going well or if they want to find a job with a higher salary.

These groups, like the National Immigration Forum, largely disagree with Vance. They argue that competing for specialized talent from around the world benefits the US economy.

“The United States has long benefited from its ability to attract talent from around the world, particularly in STEM, higher education, research, and innovation,” the National Immigration Forum wrote in a September 2026 blogpost discussing proposed changes to the H1B program. “As countries increasingly compete for highly skilled workers, policies that make the United States less attractive could strengthen global competitors.”

title: Bank governor urges John Healey to use budget to allay market fears amid bond turmoil
excerpt:
Andrew Bailey tells chancellor ‘whatever the stance of fiscal policy, it must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets’

The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, has urged the chancell...
body_text:
Andrew Bailey tells chancellor ‘whatever the stance of fiscal policy, it must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets’

The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, has urged the chancellor, John Healey, to agree a budget that reassures financial markets after the UK’s medium-term borrowing costs hit a fresh 19-year high.

With investors offloading government bonds previously considered safe havens amid fears of rising inflation, Bailey told all governments caught in the crosshairs of financial speculators that they needed to avoid market turmoil that raises the interest paid on debt.

Recent dramatic moves in government bond markets have been driven by international factors, but will increase the pressure on Healey ahead of his tax and spending announcement on 28 October.

The yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds had risen 0.06 percentage points by lunchtime in London, to 5.515%. That was the highest level since July 2007, when the global financial crisis was starting to unfold.

Yields on 20- and 30-year UK government bonds, which are known as gilts, also rose significantly, to their highest level since as long ago as 1998. Yields go up when bond prices go down.

Yields later dropped back on a day of volatile trading, but analysts said further conflict in the Middle East would push them up again as concerns increased about inflation becoming embedded in many major economies.

Meanwhile, the benchmark oil price rose by more than 5% to $105.3 a barrel amid escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast.

Diesel prices at UK pumps hit £2 a litre last week, leading to concerns among central banks that inflation will surge over the coming months, leading to higher interest rates and burgeoning government debt financing costs.

Speaking at a conference in Istanbul, Bailey said he would not meddle in government policy, but he had one observation for Healey after the recent bond rout dramatically increased UK borrowing costs.

“Whatever the stance of fiscal policy, it must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets,” he said.

Realistic commitments to rein in debt would help curb demands ‌for higher returns from investors who might sell when there were shocks like the outbreak of the Iran war, he said. “In other words, such commitments are needed more than ever when these negative shocks occur.”

Economists believe rising borrowing costs and a weaker growth outlook are likely to have wiped out around half of the £24bn buffer against Labour’s fiscal rules that Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, built up at the time of her spring statement in March – perhaps significantly more.

Healey is expected to raise taxes at the budget to partly rebuild that cushion, as well as paying for policy interventions including the six-month VAT cut on electricity bills and a modest energy support package for the poorest households.

Some economists are warning the chancellor not to go too far in rebuilding the Treasury’s headroom, however. Andrew Wishart, of Berenberg Bank, said: “Raising taxes to keep the surplus close to the size it was in the March forecast (ie to ‘maintain the headroom’) would do unnecessary damage to economic incentives.”

He argues that gilt yields are likely to come back down over the next year, with the Bank of England likely to make fewer rate rises than the four that investors currently expect.

The Bank is widely expected to raise interest rates at its November meeting to tackle surging inflation, echoing moves already made by the European Central Bank, Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan.

The bond selloff has intensified across big economies in recent days, as oil prices have soared, with no resolution of the Middle East conflict in sight.

Investors appear to be anxious about higher inflation and runaway government spending. France has been hardest hit, as Paris battles to pass a budget, but the selloff has been widespread.

Reuters reported that European Central Bank officials and eurozone finance ministers were preparing on Thursday to make representations to the French government to pass a 2027 budget to calm bond ⁠markets.

Investors are worried about the country’s large budget deficit and 2027 presidential election. Its ⁠10-year bond yield has jumped nearly 80 basis points since the start of September and hit its highest level since July 2002, just short of 5%.

An EU official said finance ministers were unlikely to make a public plea, but would call for a budget that brought down annual borrowing.

“That’s kind of a no-brainer. So I would expect this to be the main message,” the official said.

Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), has urged governments to tighten their belts in response to rising bond yields.

“My message to the world’s economic policymakers will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said, ahead of next week’s IMF annual meeting in Bangkok.

Higher yields not only push up costs for indebted governments, but have knock-on effects for borrowers across the economy, including homeowners and businesses.

The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has tried to rein in yields on the US’s long-term debt by increasing buybacks of its government bonds, known as treasuries, but the policy appears to have had little impact.

Yields on the 30-year treasuries targeted by Bessent’s policy were about 5.235% when he announced the doubling of buybacks in August, but have since surged above 5.7%.

title: Trump claims US won’t strike Iran before November midterms – live
excerpt:
President claims US won’t attack ‘at any time prior’ to elections after reports suggest White House asked Pentagon to develop strike options for before 3 November

Send us your questions on how the US...
body_text:
President claims US won’t attack ‘at any time prior’ to elections after reports suggest White House asked Pentagon to develop strike options for before 3 November

Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections

Donald Trump claimed that the US will not strike Iran “at any time prior” to the midterm elections on 3 November.

This comes after reporting from the Atlantic suggested that the White House has asked the Pentagon to develop strike options against Iranian targets that could be carried out ahead of the midterms.

On Truth Social today, the president said there were no plans to carry out attacks as long as “Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade [in the strait of Hormuz] will remain in full force and effect”.

The missive comes as the president’s approval rating sinks to a new low, according to polling this week, and gas prices remain elevated, with the average gallon still costing more than a dollar more than before the war with Iran began in February. The conflict has arguably become the most politically toxic issue plaguing Republicans ahead of the November elections, with a number of Trump-endorsed nominees in key battlegrounds calling for an end to the war to ease prices for voters.

In closing, the lawyer for the newsrooms said that it is a “very dangerous, chilling doctrine” if a journalist’s press pass is at risk “because President Trump decides something you said is false”.

However, he noted that the first amendment imbues reporters with protection while covering the government, and requested that the Judge Kelly convert the temporary restraining order of the ban to a preliminary injunction.

Kelly said that he expects to issue a ruling by Tuesday, but possibly earlier. In the meantime he extended his pause of Trump’s ban, which was set to expire today, until then.

The lawyer representing the Trump administration, Michael Velchik, argued today that there are two reasons behind banning the three outlets. First “packaging verifiable falsehoods” and failing to meet “minimum journalistic standards”, and second national security.

“We’ve never argued that this is solely and only because of national security,” Velchick said, but later conceded that there is “overlap” between the two ideas and they are not mutually exclusive.

Interestingly, Velchick argued today that it would be a tall order for the outlets to claim irreparable harm for being blocked from the White House, because of the pool members who acted in solidarity by refusing to carry television feeds while their newsrooms were blocked from the White House.

“I would ask the court to try and analyze how, in practical terms, can they say that it is irreparable,” he said.

The administration has argued that it tried to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House on national security grounds. The White House claimed that the outlets have failed to meet basic standards of “professionalism and decorum”, including allegedly publishing sensitive or classified material.

However, the lawyer representing the outlets said today in court that the government hasn’t backed up their claims that their reporting affected national security.

“They haven’t said they haven’t shown with any evidence that this was ban was implemented because of national security concerns,” Ted Boutrous said. “They haven’t shown that the ban that the reports jeopardize national security … They haven’t found that the ban helped them protect national security, and so the harm would be irreparable.”

Earlier, Boutrous argued that “one of the most important areas that journalists report on is national security, and it’s been going on in the White House and outside the White House since the beginning of our country”.

He added: “It’s extremely important for reporters to report on that andhold the government accountable.”

We’re following the key hearing in the Trump media ban case now, which is under way in DC district court.

Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing CNN, MS Now and Politico, said today that Trump has “unambiguously said” that the grounds for barring these outlets is “because of what he perceives as negative, false, bad, not positive enough reporting”.

He also repeated to Judge Timothy Kelly, the Trump-appointed judge presiding, that the outlets received “no notice whasoever” about the ban – an issue that Kelly brought up explicitly when he issued his temporary injunction two weeks ago.

Boutrous noted that Steven Cheung, the White House communications director who he described as “no shrinking violet” also issued no declaration that there was a specific problem.

“President Trump has been making these nasty comments about my clients for a long time, and suddenly there’s an emergency,” Boutrous said.

Also today, the administration announced it had launched investigations into nine universities, they allege are committing J-1 visa fraud.

These temporary visas that are often used by higher education institutions for specialized work and study exchange programs. The justice department announced these investigations into Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, University of Pittsburgh, University of Califonia Davis, Caltech, Arizona State, and Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

“Subpoenas have been served. Investigations are underway, and nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building,” said Anthony D’Esposito, the inspector general of the labor department.

Today, the Trump administration announced it would block Microsoft from a program sponsoring foreign workers for green cards – which grant permanent residency in the US.

These workers are already in the US on H-1B visas, a temporary work visa that allows US companies to hire skilled foreign workers for specialized jobs. Since returning to office last year, Donald Trump has sought to restrict the use of the program, including by imposing a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas. That order was later blocked in court.

Today, the administration said it was suspending Microsoft from the so-called Perm program, the first step employers must complete when sponsoring workers for employment-based green cards. The move would prevent Microsoft from using the process to seek permanent residency for many employees currently on H-1B visas.

“Our message to Microsoft is: you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants,” said vice-president JD Vance. “We cannot allow visa programs that were designed to ensure that American corporations had access to the best and the brightest to use them to undercut the wages of American workers.”

Vance also claimed that that foreign workers are “earning wages that are far below the average for American citizens”. However, according to a 2025 study from the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, while immigrants in the US earn 10.6% less than similarly educated US-born workers, but this is because they are concentrated in “lower-paying industries, occupations and companies”, not getting paid less for the same work.

US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has used his latest tour of Europe to voice fears over the spillover effects of the war in Ukraine.

On the third day of his tour in Europe, Rubio expressed Washington’s mounting concern over the ability of the war in Ukraine to spread, more than four years after Russia invaded the country.

In an interview with Greece’s authoritative Kathimerini newspaper – published hours before he departed Athens for Portugal – Rubio said the conflict appeared to be mired in a “strategic stalemate which is a dangerous thing,” because a negotiated settlement was still far off.

“In the meantime, we watch with great concern as escalation could happen. Just yesterday, some ships were attacked in the Black Sea through a coordinated drone attack. We’re worried about a sabotage operation in a neighboring country that can spiral out of control,” he said.

It was clear, he told the paper, that Russia was now bent on using the upcoming winter to destroy Ukraine’s electricity grid in a bid to get Kyiv to surrender.

“Meanwhile, Ukraine has grown more effective in its ability to conduct long-range strikes deep into Russia. So, we share the same concern. The whole world is going about this thing like something that could escalate and perhaps become a broader conflict.”

Rubio also predicted that Tehran was only weeks away from “facing the most cataclysmic economic catastrophe in the history of modern Iran,” saying the country’s oil shipments were about to run dry because it no longer controlled the Strait of Hormuz.

About 20% of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) is shipped through the waterway connecting the Gulf with the Arabian Sea. “Now, as it stands today, the Straits are open, and Iran does not control them. Oil shipments through the southern lane, which we cleared of mines, are now at almost 80% of pre-conflict levels. The only country that cannot reliably get oil out of the Middle East is Iran, whose shipments have all been blocked or stopped by a blockade. They’re facing crushing economic pressure, which will only grow exponentially in the next few weeks.”

Former president Barack Obama has endorsed Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee in the US Senate race in Maine.

A reminder that Jackson, a logger and former state lawmaker, replaced Graham Platner – the embattled former nominee – after he faced allegations of sexual assault and rape, which he denies.

Platner’s withdrawal from the race set off a frantic search for an alternative, and resulted in a special party convention where Jackson secured nearly all the delegates from across the state. He’ll now face the five-term Republican incumbent, Susan Collins, in November. Who, for years, has boasted her “moderate” credentials and proven unbeatable in a purple state that Trump has lost three times.

In a straight to camera video, Obama touted Jackson’s achievements as Maine senate president, said the state needs a “fighter like Troy” in Congress and emphasised Jackson’s work to protect reproductive rights in the state legislature in the wake of the Dobbs decision, which overturned the constitutional right to an abortion.

On the trail, Collins has received blowback for her 2017 vote to confirm conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh to the supreme court. In 2022, Kavanaugh joined the majority opinion overturning Roe v Wade, the landmark abortion rights protection. This year’s midterm elections mark the first time Collins is on the ballot since the ruling.

As I noted earlier, we’ll have the second debate between Jackson and Collins in Maine at 8pm ET.

Donald Trump has urged James Talarico, the Democratic nominee in the US Senate race in Texas, to debate Ken Paxton – Republican attorney general that the president has endorsed in the election.

On Truth Social, Trump described Paxton as “ready, willing, and able” to take on Talarico – the 37-year-old state representative who has been leading in several polls.

The Texas legislator’s rising star has led Trump to the Lone Star state to rally for Paxton, who he has previously disparaged for his appearance and oration, while Republican groups have poured tens of millions of dollars into the race. A Democrat hasn’t won statewide office in Texas since 1994.

The president, however, claimed on social media that Talarico is “MISSING IN ACTION!”.

“No one has seen him for an extended period of time. Where is he? What is wrong with him? Bad rumors are coming out,” Trump said of Talarico, while urging him to face-off Paxton on stage.

The Democrat’s campaign said Talarico paused in-person events at the end of September due to a flu diagnosis.

Later today, we’ll be keeping an eye on three key Senate debates ahead of the November midterms.

In Georgia, Jon Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent will face off against Mike Collins – a congressman and the Trump-backed Republican nominee at 7pm ET.

At the same time in Michigan, progressive insurgent Abdul El-Sayed, will debate Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee also endorsed by the president.

Finally, it’s the second debate in Maine in as many days. Susan Collins, the five-term Republican incumbent will spar (again) with the Democratic nominee, Troy Jackson, at 8pm ET.

A reminder that these are some of the most competitive seats in this midterm cycle. Georgia and Michigan represent two must-holds for Democrats, while Maine is a key pick-up opportunity in order to boost the party’s odds of reclaiming the upper chamber of Congress.

The federal judge who issued a temporary restraining order, pausing Donald Trump’s ban of CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House, is set to hold a hearing at 11am ET today.

Timothy Kelly, a Trump-appointee, previously blocked the president from carrying out the ban, but that is set to expire today.

Now we’ll see whether that pause is extended on the administration’s latest attempt to strip access from members of the press whose coverage it claims to be negative and inaccurate.

The three newsrooms have since requested for Kelly to extend his pause while the litigation plays out.

At the initial hearing two weeks ago, Kelly was skeptical of the administration’s argument to bar the three outlets from the White House grounds, expressing that they received no prior warning. He also pointed to existing precedent, which shows the high standards needed to prevent press-pass holders from accessing the White House – including a written notice with the reasons for denial.

Since Kelly’s injunction, there have been several reports of the affected outlets still being barred from covering the president. Most recently, a reporter from Politico was prevented from traveling on Air Force One to cover Trump’s rally in Nebraska on Monday. While CNN journalists were also stopped from also traveling on the jet at the end of September to report on the president’s trip to Tennessee.

A reminder: these outlets are part of the press pool, an almost century-old system in which news organisations take turns covering the president’s daily movements. When Trump returned to office, the White House took control of the pool rotation, which previously was managed by an independent association. Kelly’s temporary block technically doesn’t apply to Air Force One or the Oval Office – smaller spaces that only those on pool duty have access to on any given day.

Donald Trump is in Washington today. At 1.30pm ET he’ll be at the US Institute of Peace – the organization he has attempted to gut and rename after himself – to attend the American innovation summit.

The president is expected to present Elon Musk, the Tesla and Space X founder, with the medal of science. It’s a full circle moment for the pair – who began Trump’s second administration as close allies. Musk led the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, and was tasked with hollowing out large parts of the federal government, under the guise of rooting out “waste, fraud and abuse”.

However, Musk’s fidelity faltered last year when he criticized the president’s sweeping domestic policy legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill, and took issue with Trump’s attempts to rollback electric vehicle incentives. It led to a public falling-out that resembled a celebrity break-up.

However, in recent months, Musk appears to be back in the fold. He has been present as several major White House events, including the state dinner for China’s president, Xi Jinping. Musk was also recently tasked with heading up a temporary Pentagon project to analyze “the future of warfare” alongside Palmer Luckey – a key Trump ally and donor – and former House fspeaker Newt Gingrich.

Marco Rubio, the US Secretary of State, has been forced to yet again address allegations of misconduct by Kimberly Guilfoyle, America’s ambassador to Greece.

At the end of an action-packed trip, topped by what US diplomats called an historic policy speech before the Acropolis, Marco Rubio was brought face-to-face, once again, with the grubby allegations of improper behaviour by his top diplomat in Athens.

For the second time in the space of 12 days the Wall Street Journal had run a report detailing misconduct by Guilfoyle – the former fiancée of the US president’s oldest son Donald Trump Jr.

The report was published late Wednesday as Rubio was holding talks with Greek premier Kyriakos Mitsotakis. It alleged the former Fox News channel host had asked Eric Deters, a Republican donor and supporter of president Trump, to pay off a $100,000 American Express credit card bill ahead of her confirmation hearing on 9 July 2025. In exchange, Guilfoyle reportedly promised direct access to the White House and high profile officials in the Trump administration.

Early Thursday as he was about to board a plane for Portugal - the last stop in his three-day tour of Europe – Rubio was asked to comment. Acknowledging he was aware of the report - and as Guilfoyle looked on - he told reporters:

double quotation markYou guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things.

It was not the first time the foreign policy chief has been forced to address reports of misconduct swirling around Guilfoyle - or alluded to fake news in debunking them.

On Wednesday, at a press conference with Greece’s foreign minister, he was asked if he remained confident in the envoy amid mounting congressional scrutiny of Guilfoyle’s tenure following earlier allegations detailed by Journal.

Visibly irritated, Rubio shot back saying:

double quotation markThis is not the forum to address this, as simple as that. Suffice it to say, our embassy here is doing a great job. Our ambassador here has been a strong ambassador here.

Late last month the Wall Street Journal ran a report accusing the high-profile ambassador of improper behaviour around the sale of US natural gas exports to the region via Greece. The paper reported an incident in which Guilfoyle was also said to have boasted about America’s ability to undermine governments, including the Greek government, if they didn’t comply with US wishes.

Donald Trump has said he wants to develop one of his Florida golf courses into a presidential retreat where his successors can spend quiet weekends on the greens, describing it as “sort of a Camp David ” that he says would already have many of the security features needed to host presidents and world leaders.

The proposal for the retreat on Trump’s private golf course in West Palm Beach would comingle the presidency with Trump’s business ventures beyond his time in office, and is the latest example of Trump seeking ways to leave his imprint on the presidency.

“It’s a great idea, and it’ll be used a lot,” Trump said, claiming it was suggested by the United States Secret Service. “It seems that all presidents play golf.”

Worries around artificial intelligence cross party lines, with the vast majority of Americans saying the US government should prioritize keeping AI under human control and protecting workers.

A new poll from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that most Americans, 64%, think AI is developing “too fast,” while 27% say its development has been “about right” and only 8% say it’s moving “too slow.”

The risk that powerful AI models could evade human control and hurt humanity, once the stuff of science fiction, has been emerging as a more pressing concern.

Even leaders of the companies that are developing frontier AI models are calling for a slowdown so that government regulation can catch up.

President Donald Trump has pushed back against slowing down AI development because of concerns that China will gain an advantage with the technology.

Secretary of state Marco Rubio is in Portugal on the last leg of a three-nation tour of Nato allies.

Rubio arrived in Lisbon on Thursday for a brief stop on his return to Washington, a day after delivering a speech in the Greek capital of Athens urging European countries to save Western civilization by upholding the values and traditions of ancient Greece.

Rubio, who began his trip in Iceland, is expected to thank Portuguese officials for supporting US operations in the Iran war by allowing the US to use the Lajes Field air base in Portugal’s mid-Atlantic Azores islands, which is strategically located for military refueling flights.

The US Air Force has long had a base there under an agreement with Portugal. Unlike neighboring Spain, where socialist leader Pedro Sánchez refused to allow the American military to use Spanish bases to stage operations for attacks on Iran, Portugal’s center-right government granted Washington “conditional approval” to use Lajes Field.

“Portugal is a great ally, very cooperative ally of the United States and a country with which we already have a solid and growing relationship. And we visit these countries in order to reinforce those ties,” Rubio said before departing Athens. “That’s the purpose of the trip.”

As Donald Trump struggled to end the war with Iran, and the Lincoln’s deployment dragged on, reports emerged over the summer of shortages of food and basic supplies, and deteriorating mental health and morale among some crew members, including that two crew members had attempted to jump overboard.

At the time, senior Trump administration officials dismissed the reports. Hegseth claimed they “completely misrepresented” the reality, while Trump, when asked in August whether the deployment had gone on too long, responded, “Not nearly long enough” – a remark that upset some naval families.

The reports about the conditions on the Lincoln caused concern among some military health experts, veterans and families of sailors onboard, and drew outrage from Democratic lawmakers, including several who demanded more information from the Pentagon.

The Lincoln was relieved from its deployment later in August, as the USS George Washington aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East to take its place.

But in recent weeks, as the Lincoln has headed back to San Diego, a new disclosure about the carrier has renewed scrutiny. Acting navy secretary Hung Cao acknowledged last month that eight service members from the Lincoln and its strike group had attempted suicide during the deployment.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

The USS Abraham Lincoln will return home to San Diego later today after supporting the Iran war during a record long deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea.

For months, there have been widespread concerns since reports first emerged of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health onboard.

In remarks yesterday, however, US defense secretary Pete Hegseth sought to play down the issues, instead condemning “a few folks in the media” who he accused of trying to “turn” the Lincoln’s deployment “into some sort of symbol of dysfunction, or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission”.

While Trump administration officials pushed back against accounts of poor conditions, families and veterans warned that the length and intensity of the deployment were taking a toll on both those serving onboard and their loved ones.

As reports of conditions leaked out, the Lincoln soon became a flashpoint in the increasingly contentious debate over the war and, for some, a symbol of the strains and pressures the conflict has placed on the US military and the people serving in it.

Hegseth flew out to the carrier on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.

He said that “what makes the US military and the US Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you’re resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless.”

Hegseth told the crew that president Donald Trump “tracked your activities from day one and couldn’t be more proud of what you executed.”

The US carrier, with roughly 5,000 sailors and marines onboard, left San Diego in November 2025, initially bound for the Pacific and expected to return in the spring. But after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in late February, the Lincoln was redirected to the Middle East, to support US operations in the region.

In remarks in San Antonio, Texas, Donald Trump tried to channel the anti-Muslim racism that helped get him elected in 2016, by skipping straight from a dire warning that Iran would use a nuclear weapon if it had one to the wild, false claim that Barack Obama could have stopped the Ft Hood gunman, Nidal Hasan, but chose not to.

Trump repeated his false claim that the war he started with Iran in February was necessary to prevent Iran from destroying American cities like Los Angeles or San Diego in a nuclear attack. In fact, US intelligence agencies assessed in 2025 that Iran had abandoned its pursuit of nuclear weapons in 2003.

Trump’s midterm rally speech was disrupted up to a dozen times by protesters.

The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration in federal court, asking a judge in Washington to stop the president from using taxpayer funds to air a series of ads promoting himself, arguing that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda.

title: Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
excerpt:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv's allies needed to take "concrete action"

At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern fron...
body_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv's allies needed to take "concrete action"

At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.

Authorities said three people were also killed in the village of Bilenke, part of the Kramatorsk community.

Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.

Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Moscow is trying to seize as part of Russian President Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said: "This strike will not go without our response."

In a post on Telegram, he said: "Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this. React harshly - exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have caused."

Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.

Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack. It follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across Ukraine and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.

According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.

In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who together with Zelensky visited the site of the Russian strike in Pryluky, said the attack showed Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".

He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war" and told Zelensky the UK would stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes for you to prevail in this conflict".

After the deadly attack on Kramatorsk, Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the eastern front line region to move to safer parts of Ukraine.

Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.

Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched by Putin in 2022 - a claim rejected by Ukraine and its allies as baseless.

Donbas is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.

For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.

Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall.  In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.

Kramatorsk city council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".

"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it said.

Children killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 22 in block of flats

Civilians told to flee Ukraine's fortress cities as Russia bids to control Donbas

Russia has in recent weeks been launching constant air raids on the capital Kyiv, with sirens ringing virtually non-stop.

On Thursday, Kyiv police said four people were killed and two injured in the latest Russian attack on the city.

The attacks are forcing schoolchildren out of classes into underground shelters, shuttering businesses, and disrupting public transport.

Moscow's strikes on Ukraine's key infrastructure, particularly on its energy grid, are causing power outages already and are even affecting the water supply. Local water authorities in the capital warned on Thursday that pressure was dropping across the city's right bank due to power cuts.

Kyiv's metro network - which millions of residents rely on - on Thursday briefly halted all its train traffic due to a voltage drop from "external power centres". Trains later started moving again - but at greater intervals, local officials said.

Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine".

Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.

Such warnings are for now one of the only defences Ukrainians have.

Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little  chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics.

Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.

On Thursday, Russian state-run media reported that a number of websites in the country were inaccessible following a Ukrainian drone attack on a data centre of Yandex - Russia's largest search engine.

title: Campaigners led by Chris Packham urge prime minister to rethink Send reforms
excerpt:
Exclusive: Letter to PM, also signed by Sally Phillips, says reforms will unfairly remove children’s legal protections

Legal rights must be retained for children with Send

Campaigners are calling on...
body_text:
Exclusive: Letter to PM, also signed by Sally Phillips, says reforms will unfairly remove children’s legal protections

Legal rights must be retained for children with Send

Campaigners are calling on Andy Burnham to abandon the core elements of the government’s reforms to special educational needs provision, arguing they unfairly remove children’s legal protections.

A group of disabled children, parents and experts, led by the broadcaster Chris Packham, have written a letter calling for the prime minister to gut the plans laid out under his predecessor, Keir Starmer.

Starmer and Bridget Phillipson, the former education secretary, announced the sweeping reforms this year, aiming to curb the increase in legally mandated education, health and care plans (EHCPs) and save money in the long term.

Now campaigners are hoping the change of prime minister and education secretary may bring a change of heart from the government – even though officials say it is unlikely.

In the letter, published in the Guardian, the campaigners say: “The legal rights of children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) are still under threat.

“The government’s proposed … reforms would significantly reduce existing legal rights to enforceable EHCPs, parental choice of educational settings and independent routes of appeal.”

They add: “We … urge ministers to work with Send families and organisations to retain existing Send legal rights, preserve individual provision, improve accountability in the system, and retain meaningful independent routes of appeal.”

The letter is signed by 36 people, including Packham, the actor Sally Phillips, the clinical psychologist Simon Baron-Cohen and the Guardian columnist John Harris.

The reforms were announced in February after lengthy consultation by ministers with experts and Labour MPs.

Under the plans, instead of legally enforceable EHCPs, millions of pupils will be given individual support plans (ISPs), which will be agreed between parents and schools but will not be subject to independent legal appeal.

These ISPs will be administered by schools rather than local authorities, and parents who are unhappy with them will be asked to appeal to the school rather than being given recourse to an independent tribunal.

Schools will be given more resources to help support Send children, but the overall package is designed to curb the rapid escalation in costs under the current system, which has left councils in England facing a projected £6bn financial black hole in two years’ time.

However, the Guardian revealed on Thursday that the projected savings risk being undermined by a flood of new applications for EHCPs, as parents look to secure legal protections before the new system takes force.

The campaigners say they want significant changes to the proposals, including keeping the current threshold for EHCPs, allowing parents to appeal decisions at a tribunal and scrapping the assessment system proposed for ISPs.

Ministers are consulting on the measures and are expected to recommend some changes to Phillipson’s proposals.

However, those close to the process say Burnham and Lucy Powell, the new education secretary, are likely to adopt more minor modifications to reinforce legal protections rather than the wholesale changes called for by the campaign group.
