title: US stock market hits all-time high as investors bet big on AI
excerpt:
The United States stock market has hit an all-time high as excitement around artificial intelligence continues to fuel a buying frenzy on Wall Street.

The S&P 500, the benchmark stock index, closed 0...
body_text:
The United States stock market has hit an all-time high as excitement around artificial intelligence continues to fuel a buying frenzy on Wall Street.

The S&P 500, the benchmark stock index, closed 0.58 percent higher on Tuesday, topping the previous peak reached in mid-August.

The Nasdaq Composite, which is more heavily weighted towards tech stocks, also hit a record high, finishing up 0.45 percent.

Tech stocks were among the top performers, with each of the “Magnificent Seven” apart from Meta closing higher.

Amazon led the pack with a 1.95 percent gain, followed by Microsoft and Tesla, which rose 0.78 percent and 0.51 percent, respectively.

Apple and Alphabet both rose 0.22 percent, while Nvidia gained 0.14 percent.

Meta, which has risen more than 20 percent since the launch last month of its new AI assistant, Muse, fell 0.41 percent.

Other big movers in tech included Marvell Technology, which rose 5.81 percent, and Cisco, which gained 4.54 percent.

Keith Lerner, chief investment officer and chief market strategist at Truist Advisory Services in Atlanta, Georgia, said the market rally should be seen as a “technology and AI surge”.

“Every bull market has a dominant theme, and technology and AI remain this market’s dominant theme,” Lerner told Al Jazeera.

“Technology and communication services were the only two S&P 500 sectors to rise last month, while the other nine declined.”

Wall Street has shrugged off a host of challenges facing the US economy amid hyperscalers’ multibillion-dollar investments in AI.

Despite the energy crunch caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran and a sell-off of US government bonds partly driven by ballooning government debt, the market is well on track to record its fourth consecutive year of double-digit returns.

The S&P 500 has risen 14 percent so far in 2026, while the Nasdaq Composite is up 18.78 percent.

“Investors remain bullish on the prospects for AI,” Lochlan Halloway, a senior equity strategist at Morningstar Australia, told Al Jazeera.

“They are betting that the money pouring into data centres will earn a good return, and so far that belief has outweighed rising interest rates, more expensive oil and a 10-year bond yield above 5 percent,” Halloway said.

“We are positive on AI too,” Halloway added. “But the range of outcomes is wide, and the market is concentrated in a handful of companies, so the outlook for US shares, and by extension global shares, relies on the AI story continuing to deliver.”

Lerner at Truist Advisory said the market rally had the potential to continue through the end of 2026 given historical trends and expectations for strong corporate earnings.

“We do not expect a straight line higher for markets,” Lerner said.

“Still, the fourth quarter of midterm-election years has produced an average gain of 7 percent and has been positive 84 percent of the time since 1950.”

Lerner said that rising interest rates posed the biggest risk to the upward trend.

“Still, on balance, the weight of the evidence suggests this bull market still has more upside potential,” he said.

Asian stock markets fell on Wednesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong slumping in morning trading.

The Nikkei 225 in Tokyo, Kospi in Seoul and Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong were down 0.79 percent, 1.36 percent and 0.71 percent, respectively, as of 02:30 GMT.

Oil prices, which have been elevated since the start of the war on Iran, rose on Wednesday as traders weighed the fallout of fighting between forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis.

Brent crude futures for December delivery stood at $101.45 a barrel as of 02:30 GMT, up 0.87 percent.

title: Oman evacuates injured crew from attacked tanker in Strait of Hormuz
excerpt:

The On Peace tanker was struck 9 nautical miles (about 17km) off the Oma...
body_text:
Oman’s air force has evacuated 10 crew members of a Panamanian-flagged oil tanker following an attack in the Strait of Hormuz.

The On Peace tanker was struck 9 nautical miles (about 17km) off the Omani port city of Limah on Tuesday, according to the Omani Ministry of Defence. The attack set off a fire on board the vessel.

“The crew members were transported to the Khasab hospital in Musandam governorate and received medical treatment,” the ministry said in a statement on X.

It comes as security in the Strait of Hormuz continues to deteriorate amid the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.

India’s foreign ministry, the Ministry of External Affairs, said at least 12 of the ship’s 19 crew members were injured when a projectile hit the vessel as it transited the strait. Seventeen of the 19 crew members were Indian nationals, it said, as were 11 of the injured.

“The continuing incidents of attacks on shipping in the region remain a cause of deep concern for India,” the ministry said. “We reiterate our call for an immediate cessation of such attacks in the interests of peace and stability in the region.”

India is one of the largest contributors of sailors to merchant shipping worldwide. The Indian government said in July that at least 10 Indian seafarers had been killed since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February. Another attack on a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz in September also killed an Indian sailor.

Iran effectively closed the waterway after the US-Israel war began on February 28. It has frequently attacked commercial vessels that do not use its designated route in the waterway, and has said it wants to charge ships for passage.

At least seven other incidents involving tankers have been reported in the past week, according to Marisks, a shipping intelligence service.

Despite the attacks, oil exports from the Middle East have risen to pre-war levels in recent weeks.

The seven-day moving average of Middle East crude exports reached 18.3 million barrels per day (bpd) on September 30, compared with about 18 million bpd on average in the 12 months before the war, according to provisional data from Kpler, a data firm.

Still, prices remain high, with Brent crude futures rising to $101.51 a barrel on Tuesday, compared with $72.48 the day before the war began.

title: Man pleads guilty to 2023 killing of Lauren Heike on Phoenix hiking trail
excerpt:
Phoenix Police officials say they have arrested a man in connection with an attack at a North Phoenix hiking trail that killed 29-year-old Lauren Heike. (FOX 10)

Zion Teasley has pleaded guilty to th...
body_text:
Phoenix Police officials say they have arrested a man in connection with an attack at a North Phoenix hiking trail that killed 29-year-old Lauren Heike. (FOX 10)

Zion Teasley has pleaded guilty to the 2023 murder of Lauren Heike, who was found dead with multiple stab wounds along a trail in north Phoenix.

Teasley entered the plea last Friday to first-degree premeditated murder, as well as a separate sexual exploitation of a minor charge stemming from conduct dating to 2019, according to the Maricopa County Superior Court. Under the plea agreement, Teasley is expected to be sentenced to natural life in prison, and prosecutors will withdraw their pursuit of the death penalty. His sentencing is scheduled for Dec. 4.

He was also charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and first-degree burglary in 2020, but prosecutors voluntarily dismissed those charges last week as part of the plea agreement.

In the aftermath of Heike's killing, a police report revealed that Teasley had been struggling with his sexuality and gender identity, ABC 15 said. Police previously said they believed Heike's killing was a random attack, and investigators found no prior communication between Heike and Teasley, according to the outlet. He was also a former Marine recruit who was separated from recruit training just months after enlisting in 2019, the outlet said.

PHOENIX WOMAN, 29, FOUND DEAD ON HIKING TRAIL

Heike was found with 15 stab wounds after investigators said she was chased along a Phoenix trail. (Maricopa County Sheriff's Office / Phoenix Police Department)

"Our records indicate that Zion W. Teasley entered recruit training at Marine Corps Recruit Training Depot San Diego on March 25, 2019. He was separated June 17, 2019, prior to completing boot camp," the U.S. Marine Corps told the outlet.

When questioned by the police, Teasley said Heike appeared to be "what I would want to look like," according to the outlet.Investigators also uncovered a screenshot that they believed shed light on Teasley's state of mind. It read, "When I see a beautiful woman and I'm a man," ABC 15 said.

The outlet added that Teasley was fired from one of his jobs for being "aggressive toward female employees" and was "suspected of stealing merchandise."

PHOENIX POLICE ARREST SUSPECT IN CONNECTION TO LAUREN HEIKE'S DEATH

Lauren Heike, 29, was found dead along a community hiking trail in Phoenix in 2023.  (Phoenix Police Department)

Heike was killed in April 2023 when a resident found her body along a community trail, officials said. She was found with 15 stab wounds and injuries to her hands and forearms, police reported.

Investigators said DNA, surveillance video and cellphone location evidence linked Teasley to the crime.

Heike's family said they had supported prosecutors' initial decision to seek the death penalty but ultimately agreed with the plea agreement, which ensures Teasley will spend the rest of his life in prison without the possibility of release.

Detectives said surveillance footage captured a person who may be connected to Lauren Heike’s death. (Phoenix Police Department)

Based on the condition of Heike's clothes and officials finding her belongings scattered along the trail, investigators believe Heike was chased over a barbed wire fence during the attack.

"The suspect ran after Lauren and then sprinted away before returning to the location where Lauren's body was found and climbing over the barbed wire," Teasley's probable cause statement read.

Fox News Digital's Sarah Rumpf-Whitten contributed to this report.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Beau Lamarre-Condon didn’t talk about Jesse Baird to friend in lead-up to alleged murders, court hears
excerpt:
NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering his ex and Luke Davies in a Sydney terrace in February 2024

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Despite an alleged obse...
body_text:
NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering his ex and Luke Davies in a Sydney terrace in February 2024

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Despite an alleged obsession with his ex, Beau Lamarre-Condon never spoke about him to a close friend in the three months before allegedly murdering him, a jury has heard.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to murdering his ex-partner Jesse Baird and the man’s new boyfriend Luke Davies in a Sydney terrace in February 2024.

The former senior constable says the two men died in two separate violent struggles with him over his police pistol, and his subsequent efforts to dispose of their bodies were indicative of his panic about the unexpected deaths.

Much evidence in the NSW supreme court trial’s first three weeks has centred on Lamarre-Condon’s alleged growing obsession with Baird in the year leading up to the killings.

The prosecution alleges the then-police officer became infatuated with Baird after they broke off contact in November 2023, resolving to murder him.

However, Lamarre-Condon’s close friend Nicole Harvell told the court on Wednesday she could not remember any conversation with the ex-officer about Baird after the pair broke up for the final time.

That was despite her being in almost daily contact with the now-31-year-old.

Harvell, a police senior constable, recalled trying to contact her friend when she saw media reports that he was under suspicion for the two men’s deaths.

“Fuck Beau, are you ok?” she texted to Lamarre-Condon’s phone.

The sworn officer maintained under cross-examination that the accused killer had months earlier told her about enlisting his mother to help him lie to Baird.

Lamarre-Condon posted an Instagram story with a bunch of flowers and the caption: “When he’s in Melbourne but still sends you these.”

But publication was restricted to select friends that did not include Baird.

The photo was designed to imply Baird had sent flowers to the accused, despite the pair not being in a relationship at the time, Harvell said.

When Baird discovered the ruse, Lamarre-Condon spent $160 on a bouquet identical to the photo to lie to him, the officer’s friend said.

Lamarre-Condon then sent a photo to Baird showing his mother with the fresh bouquet.

The bouquet had a handwritten note to imply his mother had been the intended recipient and they were from her partner, who was in Melbourne, the jury heard.

“I recall the accused telling me his mother had written that note,” Harvell said.

title: Australia top court rules against coal mine expansion, citing climate harm
excerpt: Australia’s highest court has ruled against the expansion of a major coal mine, finding that planning authorities had failed to ensure that emissions of planet-warming greenhouse gases would be “minim...
body_text:
Australia’s highest court has ruled against the expansion of a major coal mine, finding that planning authorities had failed to ensure that emissions of planet-warming greenhouse gases would be “minimised to the greatest extent practicable”.

Environmental campaigners called Wednesday’s court decision the first climate case to reach the country’s highest court. They said it set a “binding national precedent” requiring climate damage be weighed when fossil fuel projects are considered.

In the ruling, three of the High Court’s five judges found that the expansion of the Mount Pleasant mine in New South Wales must be halted. Planning authorities, they said, were obliged to consider granting consent only with conditions ensuring that all greenhouse gas emissions were minimised, and had not done so in this case.

The case was brought by retired science teachers Wendy Wales and Tony Lonergan, who had fought for years to halt the planned mine expansion in Australia’s rural coal-digging heartland.

“Today the High Court has said what we have always known,” Wales said in a statement. “We cannot dig up coal, ship it overseas, watch it drive climate change, and then pretend the consequences have nothing to do with us and won’t be felt by us.”

The mine’s operator, Mach Energy, had sought to extend the life of the open-cut mine in the Hunter Valley by more than 20 years, to 2048, and to nearly double its annual output. Mach is owned by Droxford International, a subsidiary of Indonesia’s Salim Group.

Mach argued that coal exported and burned overseas could not be clearly linked to environmental effects felt near the mine.

The company’s proposal was initially approved by the New South Wales Independent Planning Commission. But environmental campaigners disagreed, saying every ounce of greenhouse gas released into the atmosphere made bushfires, floods and drought more likely.

“Today, the highest court in the country agreed that those decisions have to account for the damage they cause,” said Lonergan. “This isn’t the end of coal overnight. But it is the end of coal mine approvals that look the other way on climate.”

Australia is one of the world’s largest fossil fuel exporters, ranking among the top sellers of both coal and liquefied natural gas.

Anita O’Hart, a lawyer for Wales and Lonergan’s community group, said the “historic” ruling was expected to affect how future fossil fuel projects are handled.

“The High Court has confirmed that planning authorities cannot ignore the chain of causation from a project’s emissions through to real, local climate harm,” she said.

“This ruling will be applied by courts and planning authorities across Australia, and it will be studied internationally as one of the most significant domestic climate law decisions in the world.”

Mach Energy said it was “disappointed with the outcome” but accepted the court’s decision.

“We will continue to actively pursue all available options to ensure the long-term continuity of the Mount Pleasant operation,” the company said in a statement.

title: Alleged killing by Marine prompts US military to restrict off-base liberty in Okinawa
excerpt:

body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The U.S. military in Okinawa, Japan, is beginning an operational pause for 48 hours, prohibiting off-base liberty and ordering training after a Marine was arrested on suspicion of killing and robbing a woman.

Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, Okinawa Area Coordinator and commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, said in a letter on Tuesday that incidents like this "demand we pause for reflection" and that serving on the island "comes with responsibility."

"We speak often about standards and discipline. Standards are what we expect, and my standards are clear: be accountable for your actions; do the right thing, especially when no one is looking; and always be guided by our core values that govern our conduct at every rank," he wrote.

"We live, work, and socialize alongside the people of Okinawa; their home is our home. Every interaction with our neighbors either builds or undermines the trust that is essential to our team. When that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance and the security of this region. Accordingly, we will take time to think hard about discipline, standards and our alliance responsibilities," Watson added.

THAI RESORT CITY CRACKS DOWN ON PROSTITUTION AHEAD OF USS ABRAHAM LINCOLN ARRIVAL

U.S. MV-22 Osprey transport aircraft are parked at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan, on the main island of the Okinawa archipelago, southern Japan, on Tuesday, Feb. 18, 2025. (AP Photo/Hiro Komae)

The arrest of the Marine has sparked protests against the heavy American military presence on the southern Japanese island and concerns over military-related crime.

Japanese officials have also lodged a formal protest with the U.S. government. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned U.S. Ambassador George Glass and called for cooperation with the investigation, stricter discipline among U.S. personnel and measures to prevent similar incidents.

The killing could complicate Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s push to both strengthen the Japanese military on Okinawa and work more closely with the U.S. military to deter China.

The pause in operations will last from Wednesday through Friday, during which no "off-base liberty" or alcohol will be allowed. Restricting troops from leaving military bases and interacting with the local community is a common response by military leaders to major crime incidents.

Service members will receive training on standards, discipline and "our responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community," Watson said.

"This Period of Training will include discussions on liberty policy, enforcement mechanisms, alcohol awareness, Okinawan culture, and alliance responsibilities. Every member of this force must understand that individual conduct has consequences," he said.

After the training, which will begin on Friday, troops will transition into a 30-day "Period of Reflection."

NAVY SAILOR SENTENCED TO 44 YEARS FOR STRANGLING FELLOW SERVICEMEMBER IN VIRGINIA BARRACKS ROOM

Devin Jacob Ballard, a U.S. Marine who has been in custody in connection with the alleged robbery and murder of a woman on Japan's southern island of Okinawa, is sent to the Naha prosecutors' office in Japan, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. (Kotaro Ueda/Kyodo News via AP)

During this period, Watson said there will be "restrictions on liberty" to remind all military personnel that "liberty is a privilege and a collective responsibility." These restrictions will include a curfew and enhanced supervision.

"Liberty is a mission, and like any other mission it requires discipline, trust and teamwork to complete it successfully," he said. "Take care of your teammates. Hold one another accountable. Live up to the high standards that come with the uniform you wear."

Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the island’s capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack.

Security camera footage showed a man entering the hotel with the woman and later leaving alone.

A person looking out at the U.S. Marine Corps Air Station Futenma from Kakazutakadai Park in Ginowan, Okinawa prefecture. (PHILIP FONG/AFP via Getty Images)

Ballard was arrested after a patrolling officer spotted him walking later on Saturday in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 15 miles northeast of Naha. His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man seen in security footage, Kyodo News agency reported.

People in Okinawa have long opposed the heavy U.S. military presence on the island, although some have acknowledged its strategic benefit due to what is seen as a growing threat from China.

Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Now, the U.S. population on the island is nearly 80,000, with nearly 30,000 being active duty troops from all four branches of the armed forces. The Marines make up most of the service members on the island.

A rise in crime linked to U.S. military-related personnel has led to renewed protests on the island. The number of criminal cases involving U.S. military-related personnel rose from about 40 in 2020 to 101 in 2025, according to Okinawa prefectural police.

After three U.S. service members raped a 12-year-old girl in 1995, huge crowds protested the U.S. military presence on Okinawa. There was also frustration over a U.S. service member's rape of a teenage girl in 2024 and the delayed disclosure of the case.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Veterans of 'unbearable' Chinese factory in Ohio detail brutal work conditions amid top Dem's oversight visit
excerpt: Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., explains his decision to send a probing letter to the leaders of Fuyao Glass Industry Group, a CCP-linked Chinese automotive glass manufacturer with extensive manufacturing o...
body_text:
Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., explains his decision to send a probing letter to the leaders of Fuyao Glass Industry Group, a CCP-linked Chinese automotive glass manufacturer with extensive manufacturing operations across the American Midwest.

Dayton, Ohio – Former employees of Fuyao Glass America Inc., a Chinese-linked glass manufacturer that moved into an old General Motors plant in Ohio, gathered around one of the most prominent congressmen in the U.S. today to share their stories of misery, pain and neglect they claimed to have suffered while working for the CCP-linked corporation.

"My experience at Fuyao was not a good experience," Tiffany Moore, a woman who identified herself as a three-year veteran of the factory, told a group that gathered at the International Union of Electrical Workers in Dayton, Ohio, on Tuesday.

"The heat in there is unbearable; they don’t care," she told the group — a group that included Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif.

WHAT THE GOLF CART INDUSTRY CAN TEACH US ABOUT CHINA’S THREAT TO AMERICAN JOBS

Khanna, the ranking member on the House Select Subcommittee on the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), made the trek to Dayton to conduct Congressional oversight on Fuyao.

Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., conducts congressional oversight at a roundtable of union workers in Dayton, Ohio, on Tuesday Oct. 6, 2026. (Fox News/Robert McGreevy)

Khanna had previously sent Fuyao a letter asking them to submit a packet of information to his committee, including information on wage suppression, worker conditions and violating U.S. immigration and labor laws.

DEMAND TO END 'SCAM' VISA PROGRAM REPLACING AMERICAN WORKERS SURGES, WEST VIRGINIA CONGRESSMAN REVEALS

"Fuyao Glass America Inc. (FGA) has only provided a single supposed reply letter, dated September 23, that answers virtually none of the Committee’s questions in a material way and fails to include any document submissions," Khanna wrote in an Oct. 1 letter to the company’s leadership.

"Thus far, a generous interpretation of your approach toward this investigation would be that Fuyao does not appreciate Congress’s oversight function and the American system of government," Khanna wrote.

Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., hosts a union member roundtable in Dayton, Ohio. (Fox News/Robert McGreevy)

"A less generous interpretation of your lack of transparency would be that your companies have something to hide, beyond even what multiple federal investigations, documentaries, and press reports about Fuyao’s conduct have already uncovered," the letter, shared exclusively with Fox News Digital, read.

Khanna, despite requesting permission to visit the Lorraine, Ohio, factory, did not receive express permission from the company to do so. Despite the lack of response, Khanna continued to conduct his business, convening a roundtable that included a wide swath of former Fuyao workers.

BLUE STATES SET TO TRIGGER FRESH MINIMUM WAGE HIKES WITH PAY FLOORS MORE THAN DOUBLE FEDERAL RATE

Demetria Hodges, who identified herself as having worked at Fuyao for five years, explained how she believed the company went to great lengths to prevent the workers from unionizing.

"First they were trying to use scare tactics to get us to not vote for the union," Hodges said.

DAVID MARCUS: WHY JD VANCE'S RESHORING MESSAGE IS A PERFECT FIT FOR STRUGGLING SMALL TOWNS LIKE ST. CLOUD

"Then they offered a $2 an hour pay raise … which they have never given again. And that was like 10 years ago," she added.

Former Fuyao Glass employees speak about their time working for the Chinese-linked company during an Oct. 6, 2026 roundtable. (Robert McGreevy/Fox News)

An attendee named Darrell, who identified themselves as a former employee, also pointed out the company’s failure to cease operations when 57-year-old Ricky Patterson was killed in a grisly industrial accident in the factory.

LARGEST-EVER US STEEL PLANT IS COMING TO A KEY RED STATE AS TRUMP UNVEILS $15B INVESTMENT

"When that guy got smashed by … glass, we had to work the next day, we were stressed out. He was trying to load up the glass. He was a little shaky because he had just lost his mom," Darrell told the roundtable.

"They made us work," he told the group, who all expressed shock at the revelation.

title: Coyotes choose the front of a couple's Southern California cabin for an early morning scrap
excerpt: NASCAR driver Chase Briscoe joins OutKick OutDoors to explain how he developed a love for hunting and the outdoors, how his young son Brooks got involved, and why getting his kids away from screens an...
body_text:
NASCAR driver Chase Briscoe joins OutKick OutDoors to explain how he developed a love for hunting and the outdoors, how his young son Brooks got involved, and why getting his kids away from screens and outside matters to him.

The mystery surrounding why a couple's dog barks in the middle of the night at their Southern California cabin has been solved thanks to some early morning surveillance footage.

The footage revealed three coyotes right outside David and Annette Simpson's front door of their cabin in the San Bernardino Mountains. These wild animals weren't there to ask to borrow any sugar either.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

They were there to fight. And fight they did for about 40 minutes, starting at around 1 a.m. Sunday morning.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Stock image of a mountain cabin. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

The couple wasn't at home during the scrap in front of their cabin, but the action was caught on their surveillance cameras. What do you with forty minutes of a coyote fight?

Well, naturally, you don't want it to go to waste, so you post it on social media, then sit down for an interview with the local news.

"We wonder why our dog barks in the middle of the night, and now we know," Annette Simpson told KTLA.

Daytime view of the San Bernardino, Calif., mountains. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

TWO MASSIVE ALASKAN BROWN BEARS FIGHT OVER PRIME FISHING SPOT AT LAKE CLARK NATIONAL PARK

Indeed. It must be due to those rambunctious coyotes. While nature doesn’t come calling at your door every day, a dog will certainly know when it does.

They've seen bears, squirrels and other wildlife before, but not a coyote scrap on the walkway in front of the cabin. That's a new one for these two.

Are they worried about how close the coyotes were to their cabin? Not Annette. She's into it.

Two young coyote cubs play fight in a spring meadow along the edge of a forest in an urban park. (Getty Images)

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

"I think it’s pretty cool. We really enjoy watching the wildlife and just so close," she said. "Those stairs just lead right to our front door, and they came up those stairs."

They enjoy watching it, but they don’t want it messing with their own domesticated animals. Annette, who said she sometimes lets her cats out on the patio, is reconsidering after watching the footage of these coyotes.

title: New Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier melts
excerpt:
Government report finds the country could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as damaging storms and cyclones

New Zealand could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves an...
body_text:
Government report finds the country could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as damaging storms and cyclones

New Zealand could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves and catastrophic glacier melts in the near future, as greenhouse gas levels hit record highs, a new report about the nation’s climate has revealed.

Released on Wednesday, the Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026 report shows New Zealand is experiencing mounting climate pressures, which will have wide-reaching implications for the environment, native species and communities.

“The signal is just becoming clearer … there are multiple indicators that are showing increased warming and the likelihood of climate change,” Dr Alison Collins, chief science adviser for the ministry for cities, environment, regions and transport (Mcert) told the Guardian.

New Zealand’s annual average temperature has risen by 1.36C since records began in 1909, and seven of the 10 warmest years on record occurred in the last decade, the report said.

“Whilst it sounds like a small amount … it is a significant baseline shift that’s having ramifications through nature, through our communities, and through businesses and industry,” Collins said.

The report finds that as the climate heats, glaciers are shrinking. New Zealand has roughly 3000 glaciers, and they have shrunk in volume from 56 cubic kilometres in 1997 to 30 cubic kilometres in 2023, the report said.

Modelling of glacier retreat shows a high risk of further decline on the horizon. Under the “low climate scenario” – which assumes low emissions – glaciers will very likely lose between 14 and 86% of their volume by 2100. Under the “high climate scenario”, that figure rises to between 69 and 100% of their volume.

“We’re talking about substantial loss,” Collins said.

Greenhouse gases have increased to record levels in New Zealand’s atmosphere, the report shows. There was a 30% increase in carbon dioxide since monitoring began in New Zealand in 1972. Methane levels had also slightly increased in 2025 to their highest concentration ever.

“That additional heat is showing up in rising temperatures, warming oceans, rising seas, shifting rainfall patterns and more intense extremes,” the report said.

Among those extremes were heatwaves, which the report said were “very likely” to increase in frequency, length and intensity across the country. The number of days hitting more than 25C was also “very likely” to increase by 2050, which will expose people to heat-related health risks, including physical illness, disease and psychological distress.

Marine heatwaves are also becoming more pronounced and affecting some native species, the report said. In 2025, the series revealed New Zealand’s oceans were warming 34% faster than the global average which has been linked to mass sea sponge bleaching, die-offs of southern bull kelp, large scale fish standings and penguin deaths.

The three-yearly update from Mcert and Stats NZ collates statistics, data and research across five domains – air, atmosphere and climate, freshwater, land, and marine – to paint a picture of the state of New Zealand’s environment.

The report outlined a myriad of issues that will stem from continued warming, including damaging storms and cyclones that pose a risk to life, droughts affecting species and agricultural industries, sea level rise eroding infrastructure and housing and Māori communities having reduced access to culturally significant places.

Severe storms, including Cyclone Gabrielle and the Auckland floods in 2023, have battered New Zealand in recent years, causing deaths, widespread devastation and billions of dollars in costs.

New Zealand was built and developed around a relatively stable set of climate conditions and the report examines what happens when those conditions begin to change, Collins said.

“Climate change is not just an environmental issue. It’s a human story. It’s an economic story.”

title: People who live to 100 have 3 drinks in common, longevity expert says
excerpt: Red wine gets plenty of criticism, but it still appears in some blue zone diets. Coffee may also support healthy aging. Yet the top longevity drink is much simpler, according to longevity researcher D...
body_text:
Red wine gets plenty of criticism, but it still appears in some blue zone diets. Coffee may also support healthy aging. Yet the top longevity drink is much simpler, according to longevity researcher Dan Buettner.

In the world’s "blue zones" — regions such as Sardinia, Italy, and Okinawa, Japan, known for unusually high concentrations of long-lived residents — researchers have studied dietary and lifestyle habits for clues to healthy aging and longevity.

In a recent video post, longevity researcher Dan Buettner highlighted three beverages commonly consumed in blue zones — and studies offer some clues about how each may affect health and longevity.

Buettner ranked water first among his three longevity drinks.

FILTERED WATER AT SPECIFIC AGES COULD ADD MONTHS TO YOUR LIFESPAN DECADES LATER, NEW STUDY FINDS

"The indisputable, best thing you can drink to live to 100 [is] water," he stated. "People in blue zones are drinking six to seven glasses of water. You want to make sure it is purified water. Water helps lower your blood pressure, helps keep your blood thin and keeps you hydrated."

Research from the National Institutes of Health indicates that proper hydration helps prevent cellular degradation, lowers the risk of chronic heart conditions and supports healthy aging. (iStock)

Research from the National Institutes of Health has linked better hydration with healthier aging, including lower risks of chronic disease and premature death, although researchers noted that the findings do not prove cause and effect.

Other health experts note that adequate water intake supports kidney function, helps regulate blood pressure and keeps blood circulating effectively.

Coffee consumption has been associated with lower rates of diabetes and Parkinson's disease. (iStock)

Coffee consumption is another daily habit highlighted by Buettner, who said it is associated with lower rates of diabetes and Parkinson's.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Drink it black, one to two cups a day, quit by noon, it'll help you live longer," he added.

Routine coffee intake has been associated with reduced risks of type 2 diabetes and neurological conditions. (iStock)

Coffee contains antioxidants and polyphenols, plant compounds that have been studied for their potential anti-inflammatory effects. Routine coffee consumption has also been associated with lower risks of type 2 diabetes and neurological conditions.

Limiting added sugars and heavy creams can help avoid extra calories, while consuming caffeine earlier in the day may reduce its impact on sleep.

Residents in blue zone areas, like Sardinia, often consume small amounts of red wine during meals.

Buettner acknowledged that red wine's place in a longevity-focused diet is "controversial."

"I'm very well aware of all the negative press wine is getting lately, but it's consumed in the Blue Zones, and it seems to add years to life," Buettner said. (iStock)

"I'm very well aware of all the negative press wine is getting lately, but it's consumed in the blue zones and it seems to add years to life."

Red wine contains plant compounds such as resveratrol and flavonoids, which have been studied for their potential cardiovascular effects. However, experts have increasingly questioned whether any benefits attributed to red wine outweigh the known risks of alcohol.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Alcohol consumption has been linked to numerous health risks, including an increased risk of at least seven types of cancer, according to the U.S. Surgeon General.

People with underlying health conditions or those taking medications should consult a healthcare professional before making significant dietary changes.

Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: A beautiful Himalayan bird is changing its voice due to human activity, research shows
excerpt:
The male monal has distinctive green, blue and copper plumage

A sharp increase in human activity is having an impact on the way a Himalayan bird lives and communicates, two studies by Indian research...
body_text:
The male monal has distinctive green, blue and copper plumage

A sharp increase in human activity is having an impact on the way a Himalayan bird lives and communicates, two studies by Indian researchers have found.

The monal, a pheasant native to Himalayan mountain forests, is deeply woven into the region's cultural, folklore and identity. The eye-catching monal - the male has distinctive green, blue and copper feathers - is the state bird of India's Uttarakhand state and the national bird of Nepal, reflecting its cultural significance across the Himalayas.

But studies show that infrastructure development and tourism are squeezing its habitat, while increasing noise is altering how it communicates with potential mates and rivals.

Researchers from Uttarakhand conducted two separate studies over five years which flagged key threats to the bird.

One study found that the birds are forced to move higher in the mountains as their natural habitat in the alpine meadows above the tree line get crowded. The other says the monal is changing its pitch to cut through human noise in a busy valley.

"These two studies give a useful warning for other more vulnerable species - if the monal is forced to change both its voice and its address, how are the more sensitive species responding?" says Vishal Singh, an environmental practitioner working on ecology and climate issues in the Himalayas.

Dr Rajeev Lochan, lead researcher of both studies, told the BBC that they chose to study the monal as the bird has a narrow habitat range - it moves seasonally between the lower montane zone - an ecological belt found on the lower slopes of the mountains - and high-elevation alpine zones. This, he says, makes it a key indicator of ecosystem health in the north-western Himalayas.

"If the species is facing issues on this particular landscape, there might be a chance that the ecological disturbances are affecting other birds too," said Lochan.

Found high in the Himalayas, the monal lives in alpine meadows above the forests

The monal, researchers say, can be seen as a stand-in for the health of a fragile Himalayan ecosystem pushed to a tipping point due to unregulated tourism and heavy urbanisation.

While the region has always drawn tourists, trekkers and researchers given its scenic landscape and biodiversity, rapid infrastructure expansion in the past decade has made more places accessible, increasing footfall and disrupting the wildlife. This, coupled with mounting human pressures, suggests that climate change is emerging as another major threat to the region's already vulnerable biodiversity.

"There are a lot of factors at play but at a broader level, the problem is that the economic development of the region is not aligned to its ecological integrity," Singh said.

The Himalayas are melting faster - and India's economy is 'at risk'

Why the mighty Himalayas are getting harder and harder to see

According to the first study, climate change is projected to continue shrinking and destabilising the Himalayan monal's habitat across the Indian Himalayas through 2100 under multiple climate scenarios.

Currently, the birds are found in alpine meadows, located high in the mountains above the forests, which form some of the Himalayas' most important seasonal grazing and biodiversity-rich habitats.

The researchers modelled how climate change could shift the monal's suitable habitat across the Indian Himalayan region in the states of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. It was based on the kind of global climate models and emissions scenarios used for assessments by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN's climate science unit.

"These birds are now slowly moving upwards in the Himalayas as the snow is melting and vegetation is growing, making the area accessible to them. They are anyway being pushed upwards as their natural habitats in alpine meadows are being encroached upon by humans," Lochan said.

The model assumes that the bird needs the current climate set-up that exists in alpine meadows in the future too, a reasonable but not certain assumption.

The birds' seasonal migration may become increasingly difficult as changes in climate may force them to move to higher elevations on hills, to smaller and fragmented areas. Their population would be scattered in disconnected pockets, which reduces chances of breeding between groups and increases their risks of long-term decline or local extinction, which is already a threat, the study says.

A male Himalayan monal displays its iridescent plumage during a courtship ritual aimed at attracting a female

The second study, also conducted by Lochan, Dinesh Kumar Sharma and Anand Kumar, who work at the Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University, focuses on the bird's behavioural changes. They conducted the study in two valleys in Kedarnath Musk Deer Sanctuary in Uttarakhand - at Chopta, a tourist spot with busy traffic and visitors, and the largely quiet Madmaheshwar.

They recorded more than 700 monal calls across both sites using microphones and passive recording devices and then measured pitch, call length and background noise levels for a year from April 2023.

Birds in noisy environments consistently produced calls with significantly higher peak frequencies compared with those in quieter habitats, the study said.

The researchers found subtle changes in the monal's pitch that could be picked up by recording devices but might go unnoticed by the human ear.

"This does not mean that the species has undergone a permanent or evolutionary change in its vocal frequency; rather, our findings suggest behavioural flexibility in response to different acoustic environments," Lochan said.

Compared with the birds in Madmaheshwar valley, the monal in Chopta also produced shorter call durations likely to cut through low-frequency human noise from traffic and tourist footfall.

Bird calls are one of the most sophisticated forms of sound-based communication in the natural world, and significant changes can interfere with, among other things, their mating success.

"When a species must raise its pitch to be heard over tourist traffic, or climb higher as meadows turn crowded, it reveals how human pressure is rewriting the rules of life in the Himalaya," says Anjal Prakash, a public policy professor at FLAME University and contributor to IPCC reports.

Lochan says he and his team consider this a preliminary study and hope to expand the scope and depth of it.

The research comes with the caveat that it is not conclusive on ecological consequences, and more research is needed. But together, the two studies signal broader ecological stress across the Himalayas.

"In listening to the monal, we hear the Himalayas asking for space, silence and care," says Prakash.

title: ‘We are desperate’: Venezuela’s power cuts fuel growing public anger
excerpt:
Power cuts have spiked since the start of the year, fuelling protests against the government of interim President Delcy Rodriguez.

The hum of the kidney dialysis machine that Onasis Munoz is connecte...
body_text:
Power cuts have spiked since the start of the year, fuelling protests against the government of interim President Delcy Rodriguez.

The hum of the kidney dialysis machine that Onasis Munoz is connected to suddenly stops. The fluorescent lights overhead flicker out, and his room at a clinic in Valencia, Venezuela, is plunged into darkness.

It is not the first time a power cut has interrupted one of the three weekly sessions Munoz needs to do the work his failing kidneys can no longer do, filtering waste and excess fluid from his blood.

For years, electricity would go out every couple of days across parts of Venezuela's Carabobo state.

But in recent months, Munoz said, the outages have grown to be daily, lasting around seven hours. The clinic's emergency batteries have since been depleted, and its backup generator no longer works.

He explained that the frequent power failures have disrupted his treatment. His health has slumped as a result.

"I arrive home, exhausted, as if I had run a marathon," the 34-year-old said.

But often there is no electricity there either, and recent weeks have been sweltering. "I can't switch on the air conditioning. I cannot rest because of the heat and the mosquitoes. There's no relief," Munoz said.

Across Venezuela, the prolonged outages are riling locals, as the electricity supply to homes, businesses and essential services becomes unstable.

Some of the cuts are deliberate, as the government of interim President Delcy Rodriguez rations electricity.

The resulting frustration has spilled onto the streets, where demonstrators hold "cacerolazos" – a traditional form of protest that involves banging pots and pans.

Some have gone as far as blocking roadways and setting tyres on fire. The electricity crisis has also raised concerns about how the government is managing the country's vast oil supply, a key source of income for the country.

"We are desperate. We cannot understand how a country so rich in resources can be practically left in the dark," said Patricia Cueva, a lawyer from Maracaibo, the capital of oil-rich Zulia state.

"We cannot rest. We cannot work. Our children cry."

A recent study by ANOVA Policy Research, a consultancy firm, found that 62.8 percent of Venezuelan households – or nearly two out of every three families – experienced daily electricity cuts in 2026, compared with 37.1 percent in 2024.

Only 6.9 percent reported a continuous supply of electricity.

The energy crisis has its roots in multiple causes. Previous governments have blamed foreign sanctions for weakening Venezuela's economy.

The Rodriguez administration, meanwhile, has cited the climate phenomenon El Niño for the crisis. Some 90 percent of Venezuela's electricity is generated by hydropower, making the system vulnerable to extreme heat and drought.

But energy specialist Nelson Hernandez is among the Venezuelans pointing a finger at the government for this year's surge in outages.

Hernandez acknowledges that climate conditions can have an impact on electricity production. But he underscored that Venezuela's electricity crisis is not a "random event".

"Practically the entire crisis stems from the systematic neglect of the infrastructure," he told Al Jazeera, pointing to what he called "profound failures" in management, lack of strategic planning and ageing technology.

He also signalled that shifting government policies towards oil extraction plays a key role.

Venezuela sits on the largest proven oil reserves in the world.

Much of the oil industry was nationalised, but that started to change in January, after the US conducted a military operation to abduct and imprison Venezuela's then-President Nicolas Maduro.

Since then, relations between Washington and Caracas have shifted. Under pressure from US President Donald Trump, Rodriguez – Maduro's former vice president – has implemented reforms to allow greater foreign investment in the country's oil sector.

Trump, meanwhile, has eased restrictions on the oil's export and expanded the US role in the industry.

The result has been an uptick in output. Oil production in Venezuela has risen by almost 30 percent this year, from 924,000 barrels per day in January to 1.201 million in August, according to the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).

As Venezuela revives its dilapidated oil industry, Hernandez says increased production is putting pressure on an already strained electricity system.

"Because electricity supplies to oil fields cannot be rationed without jeopardising oil production, the burden of adjustment and the power cuts fall directly on the residential and commercial sectors," he said.

Hernandez estimates the oil industry requires around 1,600 megawatts or more for extraction, pumping, transportation and refining.

The Rodriguez government says it is working to stabilise the system, with plans to add 1,300 megawatts of generation in the final quarter of the year.

It has also put in place legal measures that compel energy companies to invest in their own electrical infrastructure, to lessen the strain on the public power grid.

But industry experts say lasting solutions require major investments to repair ageing power plants, while building more locally generated and renewable power.

For families and businesses who can afford them, backup generators provide some respite during outages. But many cannot afford them and are forced to find other ways to cope.

"My family owns a bakery, and with the constant power cuts, it is impossible to maintain consistent production," said Manuel Reyes of Naguanagua, in Venezuela's Carabobo state.

"There are days when we stay open until after midnight to make the most of the hours when there is electricity and produce something to sell."

Residents across several states who spoke to Al Jazeera said the prolonged power cuts were taking a toll on their mental health.

Mileidy Blanco, who lives in Maracay in the state of Aragua, gets up before dawn at 4am to prepare the day's food for her family before the electricity goes out.

But she said she is increasingly worried about her six-year-old daughter, who is showing signs of stress.

Recently, the electricity went out at her daughter's school, then at home and again at her dance class.

"She broke down; she couldn't take it anymore. She started crying, asking how long the lights were going to be out and how long this would last," Blanco told Al Jazeera.

Blanco took her daughter to a psychologist, who advised her to keep the child occupied during outages with board games and trips to the park.

"Her only concern should be getting good grades, studying, doing her homework, cleaning her room," Blanco said.

Instead, when the power goes out, she has noticed that her six-year-old reaches for pots and pans. She bangs along with the cacerolazo demonstrations outside in the streets – protests that show no sign of stopping.

title: Privacy watchdog launches probe into China-based company behind Kmart ‘pervert glasses’ app
excerpt:
Commissioner said Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the smartglasses, failed to respond to her inquiries

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Aus...
body_text:
Commissioner said Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the smartglasses, failed to respond to her inquiries

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Australian privacy regulator has opened an investigation into the China-based software company behind the HeyCyan app in Kmart’s $89 smartglasses, following public outrage over the covert use of the devices.

In August, Guardian Australia reported Kmart had sold out of the Anko-branded discount version of Meta’s smartglasses that can capture images and record high-definition video, which led to widespread concern and calls to ban or restrict their use.

A GetUp petition has had more than 55,000 signatures calling to restrict the use of what has been labelled as “pervert glasses”, and councils around the country have looked to ban the glasses in public spaces such as swimming pools. The federal government is also considering a restriction on use in government workplaces.

The Australian privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, was asked by the attorney general to assess the privacy implications of the glasses at the time.

Kind wrote to Kmart and BDI Technology, retailers for the glasses, as well as Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the glasses. She also wrote to Meta – for its Ray-Bans glasses – and Google which is planning its own smartglasses.

In a blog post on Wednesday, Kind announced an investigation has been opened into Shenzhen Qingcheng after it failed to respond to inquiries, “as well as concerns arising from third party analysis of the technology itself as well as the entity’s privacy policy”

None of the other companies will be investigated as part of this process, Kind said.

The privacy commissioner also highlighted the difficulty in applying privacy law to individuals who may use the devices given the privacy act only applies to companies and Commonwealth agencies – not individuals.

“Retailers that sell smart glasses – for example on an e-commerce website – or companies that manufacture them, may not have any Privacy Act obligations if they do not collect any personal information with respect to those devices,” Kind said.

“Instead, the entity providing the software at use in the device is likely to be the entity that collects and holds the information for the purpose of privacy law.”

Kind said that potential changes to the privacy act proposed by the government would strengthen how privacy law would apply to surveillance wearables such as smartglasses.

“The most substantial change will be the replacement of the ‘reasonably necessary for an entity’s functions and activities’ test with a ‘fair and reasonable’ test,” she said.

“The new test will require an entity to look at a range of factors, including the extent to which an individual had genuine choice in the collection of their personal information, as well as the best interests of the child where children are involved.”

Kind said she hoped the community would “find comfort” in the proposed reforms as it would raise the bar over what personal information smartglasses can collect.

“These reforms are likely to become increasingly necessary as we face subsequent generations of surveillance wearables and connected devices, from personal assistant gadgets to ambient recording badges.”

Researchers at the University of Sydney in August analysed 350 publicly-available Instagram videos shot on smartglasses from around the world during 2023 to 2026, showing what they said was “a shift to discreet, point-of-view recording that is difficult for bystanders to detect”.

In a subset of these videos, about 60% of interactions could be classified as potential harassment, with subjects visibly uneasy or attempting to disengage.

Canterbury-Bankstown and Sydney City are among the councils in Sydney to have banned the glasses from some venues, as well as Brisbane in Queensland, and Yarra city council in Melbourne.

Shenzhen Qingcheng was approached for comment.

title: Ikea to pilot online buyback service for secondhand furniture
excerpt:
Service to be tested in Spain and Portugal this year, with a UK rollout if successful, as pre-loved markets boom

Ikea is to test an online version of its buy-back service where the retailer offers vo...
body_text:
Service to be tested in Spain and Portugal this year, with a UK rollout if successful, as pre-loved markets boom

Ikea is to test an online version of its buy-back service where the retailer offers vouchers for unwanted secondhand furniture.

The service will be tested in Spain and Portugal before the end of December and will be launched in the UK if it proves successful. Ikea already offers buy-back in stores, including in the UK. The online version will extend it to a much wider audience, with Ikea predicting pre-owned goods are likely to grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next year

The new plan emerged as the world’s largest furniture retailer takes on Vinted and eBay with its own secondhand online marketplace which launches in the UK this week.

The platform, which is already online in other countries including Spain and Portugal with bestsellers including the Kallax shelving system and Malm chest of drawers, will enable shoppers signed up to the Swedish company’s membership scheme to connect directly to one another to buy and sell pre-owned Ikea items locally.

The UK service will be free initially, but a “buyer protection fee” of about 5% of an item’s price will be introduced in time. At launch, buyers and sellers will arrange collection or delivery directly with one another through the marketplace. Ikea said it is exploring ways to make delivery easier in future.

“The secondhand market is growing and growing. It is now really significant,” said Greg Lucas, sustainability manager at Ikea’s UK & Irish division. “Secondhand browsing and shopping is now mainstream.

“The way people furnish their homes has changed. Whether they are moving, redecorating or looking for a particular piece, more customers are considering pre-owned furniture alongside new and are actively searching for items that can help create a home that feels personal to them.”

The secondhand home products market is now worth more than £4.5bn in the UK and is growing at about 6.5% annually. Ikea said its products accounted for about 9% of furniture sold on secondhand marketplaces in the UK.

Ikea said it was making the sale of used versions of its products easier by providing pre-filled product descriptions and price suggestions. The company also offers sellers 15% extra on the price of the item sold if they agree to be paid in the form of an Ikea gift card.

The change is part of a revolution in retail, where shoppers of all ages are now prepared to consider secondhand items.

In 2025, 63% of UK consumers bought products through reselling platforms, up from 51% in 2024.

The trend has boosted sales at Vinted, which began as a clothing resale site but is now expanding into homewares and electronics, as well as at Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree and smaller, more upmarket sites such as Vinterior.

The US secondhand site eBay recently bought UK fashion seller Depop for $1.2bn (£900m). Preloved items now make up about a 10th of global fashion sales.

There is heavy competition for the secondhand market, with the electrical goods retailers Currys and AO, for example, both selling pre-owned items.

AO expanded its secondhand position after acquiring MusicMagpie, which sells refurbished electronics and secondhand video games, in 2024. It recently also bought camera specialist Jessops, which controls the Camera Jungle secondhand site.

title: Christa Pike lawyers say she is speaking one week after failed execution
excerpt:
Lawyers for Christa Pike say she is awake and able to speak after her botched execution attempt by the state of Tennessee on September 30.

Tuesday’s statement marks the first public indication that P...
body_text:
Lawyers for Christa Pike say she is awake and able to speak after her botched execution attempt by the state of Tennessee on September 30.

Tuesday’s statement marks the first public indication that Pike’s condition has improved after she was transported to a Nashville hospital after receiving two doses of pentobarbitol, lethal injections intended to end her life.

Her failed execution has sparked debate about the use of the death penalty in the United States. Pike is thought to be the first person to have survived such an injection in the country.

“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care,” Pike’s lawyers said in a statement.

“Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery.”

The statement also expresses gratitude to medical workers who the lawyers say have “treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her”.

Pike’s lawyers had previously stated that she was unconscious and on a ventilator. They described her arms as “swollen, burned and blistered” by the failed execution.

Pike was convicted and sentenced to die in 1996 for her participation in the murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18 years old. Two co-defendants received lesser sentences.

Pike’s defence lawyers had pointed to her mental health struggles in their attempts to commute her sentence. But the Slemmer family had advocated for the death penalty, pointing to the violent nature of the 19-year-old’s murder.

Accounts of Pike’s failed execution describe her kicking off the sheet covering her body and, at one point, appearing to snore. She reportedly expressed feeling pain as the lethal injections were administered.

The incident has brought attention to the prevalence of botched executions in the US criminal justice system.

Critics have argued that botched executions — defined as those that deviate from established procedures through unforeseen issues, delays or administrative incompetence — can cause unnecessary pain and suffering for those being put to death.

Citing the researcher Austin Sarat, the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit, estimates that 3 percent of executions in the US from 1890 to 2010 were botched.

title: Sarah Macdonald returns to ABC radio after being sacked in 2024
excerpt:
Manager who removed Macdonald announces she will replace the late James Valentine from March

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Two years after her shock axing, the ABC has ...
body_text:
Manager who removed Macdonald announces she will replace the late James Valentine from March

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Two years after her shock axing, the ABC has backflipped and reinstated ABC Radio presenter Sarah Macdonald to Sydney’s local radio schedule, where she will replace the late James Valentine from March.

The manager who had removed Macdonald without explanation, ABC director of audio Ben Latimer, announced her return on Wednesday to take on the afternoons slot.

“We’ve heard just how much 702 ABC Sydney listeners have missed Sarah, and I’m delighted she has agreed to return” Latimer said.

“There’s something special about Sarah taking on Afternoons. She knew James well, she knows the audience, and she understands what the program means to them. I’m really looking forward to hearing her make Afternoons her own.”

The popular ABC Sydney mornings presenter was sacked in November 2024, sparking an outcry from fellow presenters and listeners.

Macdonald announced her departure on air, telling listeners in 2024: “Well, here’s the news from me in terms of disappointment. Listen, I’m not going to be on the radio with you next year, the ABC has decided not to renew my contract here at Mornings.

“I am proud of what I’ve done. The ratings are up. I’ve broken lots of stories. Had the first interview with the new governor general. I got the premier of New South Wales to regularly take your calls. Led the election coverage, led the move to our Parramatta studios.”

Valentine, a broadcaster and saxophonist, died in April, three months after retiring from 25 years of hosting Sydney’s Afternoons program.

Macdonald confirmed she received a text from ABC managing director, Hugh Marks, on April Fool’s Day asking for a meeting.

“I have missed the ABC listeners’ wit and wisdom,” Macdonald said. “I thank them for their support, and I look forward to hanging out again. I will do my best to inform, entertain and be with listeners as we together try to make sense of the big and the small issues in life.”

The move also adds one woman to the ABC’s all male line-up from Breakfast through to Drive in 2026 after Chris Bath was replaced with a male presenter, Thomas Oriti.

At the time of her axing, then Media Watch host Paul Barry said on X: “I can’t believe this. I’m hearing that #ABC has dumped Sarah MacDonald from ABC Sydney. IMHO she’s brilliant, one of the best things on radio. WTAF?”

Outgoing drive presenter Richard Glover expressed the shock ABC staff felt on his show.

“The news today that the management here had decided not to renew [Sarah’s] contract has left our little family here, well, shell-shocked is the only word really. We were all just so taken aback, shocked, surprised, amazed, aghast, you know, choose any word you like, really.”

title: LA and San Diego residents ‘horrified’ by Trump’s comment: ‘obsessed with us’
excerpt:
As Angelenos bemoan ‘sad situation’, those in San Diego say remark a ‘disservice’ to town with multiple naval bases

Donald Trump’s extraordinary implication that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and...
body_text:
As Angelenos bemoan ‘sad situation’, those in San Diego say remark a ‘disservice’ to town with multiple naval bases

Donald Trump’s extraordinary implication that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego have sparked condemnation across the political spectrum. As residents of the two major west coast cities awoke on Tuesday to another sweltering day in a record-breaking heatwave, the president’s comments sent blood boiling even higher.

Jessica, a 28-year-old Los Angeles hair stylist, was scrolling through social media early on Tuesday morning and was shocked to see that Trump had just suggested Iran should decimate her home town.

For Jessica, who declined to be identified by her full name because she fears for the safety of her Mexican-born parents, the comments marked a new low for a president who had already spent years attacking immigrant families like hers.

“I was just thinking what the fuck is wrong with him?” she said while waiting for a Waymo outside grocery store in LA’s Koreatown neighborhood. “He hates us. He hates LA. He hates any Democratic state ... It’s just a really sad situation.”

In southern California, Trump’s unprecedented musing before a cheering crowd at a Nebraska rally on Monday night – that perhaps a foreign power should decimate two of the country’s best-known cities – has been met with reactions ranging from deep hostility to dismissive incredulity. Gavin Newsom, the state’s governor, called the remarks “dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs”.

Perhaps most of all, California residents see it as a sign of the president’s fixation on tearing down west coast progressivism and diversity, most visibly through the deployment of national guard troops in Los Angeles during a series of brutal ICE raids in 2025.

During a bustling lunch service at Grand Central Market, a food hall in downtown LA, tourists and residents milled between taco stands and dumpling stalls. Many had yet to hear of the president’s threats, until asked by a reporter. One of those who had was Jens Midthun, a downtown resident who often stops at the market for coffee.

“Trump has tried to paint Los Angeles as a dystopia despite it being a wonderful place,” said Midthun, sipping an iced coffee under a shaded outdoor table as the temperature approached the triple digits. (Midthun serves as the president of the downtown LA neighborhood council, but was speaking only on behalf of himself.)

“It reminded me that the president is obsessed with us – obsessed with California, obsessed with Los Angeles,” Midthun said. “We try not to think about him and yet, here he is with Los Angeles’s name right there in his mouth.”

Trump’s remarks have sparked a particularly strong reaction in San Diego, which is home to roughly a quarter-million veterans and has one of the largest concentrations of military personnel in the US.
  “His statement was so irrational, it’s hard to explain exactly what he was saying, but it sounded like he was willing to give us up,” said Gil Field, communications director for San Diego Veterans for Peace, a group that opposes the war. “It’s horrible and we’re horrified.”
  The military supports nearly 357,000 local jobs in the region, representing $61.3bn of San Diego county’s economy, according to a report released last year. Defense spending accounts for 22% of San Diego’s gross regional product and the area is home to multiple naval bases and Marine Corps stations, with one out of four active-duty marines based in San Diego.

“This is a military town, so you’ve got bipartisan objections to his comments,” said Field, who noted that there were always concerns that San Diego could be targeted in war due to the heavy military presence. “So for him to say this about San Diego is particularly galling. He did San Diego a disservice.”

Jim Desmond, a Republican naval veteran running for a congressional seat in San Diego, also offered a pointed rebuke.

“I served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war. Our job is to keep Americans safe, stand up to our enemies, and make sure a threat like that never becomes reality,” Desmond said on X. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”

Back in Los Angeles, far from the negative fantasies that Trump spins in his speeches, Midthun sees an economic powerhouse and vibrant cultural center sandwiched between the beach and the mountains, and enriched by some of the largest diaspora communities from across the world – South Korea, Mexico, El Salvador, Armenia and even Iran.

“The president keeps talking about us, and talking about us,” Midthun said. “He’s got a lot of issues to solve. He should work on those issues instead of obsessing over the beautiful, great people of Los Angeles.”

title: Record high temperatures as southern California swelters under heatwave
excerpt:
Several cities shatter temperatures for time of year as extreme heat warnings in place along California coast

An unprecedented heatwave has gripped southern California, boosting temperatures 15 to 20...
body_text:
Several cities shatter temperatures for time of year as extreme heat warnings in place along California coast

An unprecedented heatwave has gripped southern California, boosting temperatures 15 to 20 degrees above normal for autumn.

Monday was a notably sweltering day for several cities.

Downtown Los Angeles saw a record high of 104F (40C), breaking the previous 5 October record of 101F (38.3) in 1953, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). About 30 miles south of Los Angeles, residents of Santa Ana experienced a record 106F (41.1C) day, up from the past daily high of 103F (39.4) in 1953, the agency also reported.

Extreme heat warnings were in place along the coast from Santa Barbara to San Diego through Thursday, as health authorities advise the region’s millions of residents to limit their outdoor activity and stay hydrated.

The NWS has attributed the blistering spell to a ridge of high pressure, when hot air is trapped over a region.

In San Diego and Los Angeles, the NWS has forecasted overnight temperatures hovering in the mid to upper 70s, which the agency noted provides only little relief.

The unusual spell of extreme heat has set records not only for its sweltering temperatures, but also its prolonged length.

This past week, Los Angeles recorded four consecutive days of 100F or more, marking the longest streak of triple-digit temperatures in October.

California’s coastal areas are expected to cool starting on Thursday with rain in the forecast for next week, according to the NWS. The state’s interior regions may also see cooler temperatures on Friday and Saturday.

title: Costco rolls out new Disneyland ticket deal but there's a catch for parkgoers
excerpt:
‘Outnumbered’ reacts to reports that Costco is becoming an unexpected dating hotspot as singles look to make face-to-face connections while shopping.

Disneyland visitors have a new ticket option that...
body_text:
‘Outnumbered’ reacts to reports that Costco is becoming an unexpected dating hotspot as singles look to make face-to-face connections while shopping.

Disneyland visitors have a new ticket option that bundles park admission with other perks — but there are some restrictions that travelers may want to know about.

Costco is offering a two-day Disneyland Resort Park Hopper ticket with Lightning Lane Multi Pass and a $60 dining card for $329.99 at select locations in California.

Disneyland Resort officials confirmed the offer to Fox News Digital, saying it rolled out last week at select Costco stores across the state.

DISNEYLAND CRACKS DOWN ON GUESTS WITH SWEEPING NEW RESTRICTIONS, SPARKING BACKLASH

The resort regularly makes limited-time ticket offers available throughout the year, including through third-party retailers, according to Disneyland Resort officials.

The Costco package has since caught the attention of theme park fans online as travelers compare the price with the cost of purchasing tickets directly from Disneyland.

Costco is offering a two-day Disneyland Resort Park Hopper ticket with Lightning Lane Multi Pass and a $60 dining card for $329.99 at select locations in California. (iStock)

In a recent Instagram post, one theme park content creator highlighted the $329.99 price and the included Lightning Lane access and dining card.

"Costco has a Disneyland deal right now that is actually WORTH talking about!" the user wrote.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

By comparison, a two-day Park Hopper ticket is currently listed at $445 for one adult on Disneyland's website, before adding Lightning Lane — though pricing is subject to change.

That puts the Costco package about $115 below the currently listed two-day Park Hopper price, although the two options come with different terms and restrictions.

The resort regularly makes limited-time ticket offers available throughout the year, including through third-party retailers. (Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images)

The offer also comes as Disneyland adjusted some of its ticket prices this week.

Mid-tier single-day tickets increased by $5, while the least expensive $104 ticket and the highest-priced $224 ticket remained unchanged, according to the Los Angeles Times.

The cost of Lightning Lane can now reach $38, up $1, while the Park Hopper add-on for single-day tickets increased by $5 to $10, depending on the date, the outlet reported. Multi-day ticket prices were unchanged.

Hugh Johnston, CFO of The Walt Disney Company, speaking at the recent Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference in San Francisco, said the company is keeping ticket prices accessible for younger families by offering lower rates during off-peak value periods.

Disneyland visitors have been increasingly concerned about ticket prices as the cost — with airfare, hotel accommodations, restaurants and souvenirs — can rise quickly. (Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register/Getty Images)

"It's something that we're acutely sensitive to because we want to make sure we continue to bring young families, in particular, into the parks and develop that Disney love, right?" he said.

"So we're super sensitive to the fact that, particularly in the value times of the year, we keep those ticket prices relatively low so that we can actually encourage those young families to come in," he added.

"We want to make sure we continue to bring young families, in particular, into the parks."

The Costco ticket can be used between Oct. 2 and Dec. 18, according to information shared by the Instagram user.

Once a guest uses the ticket for the first time, the second park day must be used within 13 days, the video said.

Theme park reservations are also required for each visit, and the ticket is nonrefundable, according to the information shared online.

The same person must use both days of the ticket, meaning the two visits cannot be split between different travelers.

Once a guest uses the ticket for the first time, the second park day must be used within 13 days. (David McNew/Getty Images)

The offer is currently limited to select Costco locations in California, Disneyland Resort officials told Fox News Digital.

The package has generated mixed reactions among Disney fans online, with some questioning the cost of park visits and others praising the bundled price.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Sadly, that's still not affordable for us right now," said one person on Reddit.

Others were more enthusiastic about the offer.

"That's actually a pretty good deal," one user wrote.

Fox News Digital reached out to Costco for further comment.

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: 'Happy Days' star Anson Williams shares shirtless selfie at 77 with a defiant message about aging
