Podcaster and comedian Theo Von is one of the major podcasters who interviewed Trump, but has since been critical of his agenda in office. (Theo Von YouTube channel)

Fox News' Emma Bussey and Michael Sinkewicz contributed to this report.

Alexander Hall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Alexander.hall@fox.com.

title: Dutch royal house helped slave trade to survive, study finds
excerpt:
A historical study has found that the Dutch royal house benefited from the country’s colonial policies in past centuries and helped the slave trade to survive.

The in-depth study, commissioned by Kin...
body_text:
A historical study has found that the Dutch royal house benefited from the country’s colonial policies in past centuries and helped the slave trade to survive.

The in-depth study, commissioned by King Willem-Alexander and conducted by Leiden University, showed the House of Orange-Nassau “actively supported Dutch colonialism for centuries, but only rarely determined colonial policy”, according to the university’s statement, published on Friday.

“The involvement of the House of Orange-Nassau was wholehearted and without any real reservations,” Dutch historians and human rights experts concluded after a three-year study looking at the period from 1600 to the present.

“The research leaves us in no doubt that the House of Orange shares responsibility for the survival over the centuries of the Dutch slave trade and slavery,” the study said, noting that most of the rulers showed no objections to slavery.

King Willem-Alexander said on Friday he was personally affected by the “explicit” conclusions of the study.

“It is a painful and confronting conclusion. A conclusion that affects me, even though I am three generations removed,” Willem-Alexander said in a speech at the presentation of the research.

“We know the effects of colonialism and slavery are still being felt today. Discrimination and economic exploitation unfortunately happen every day,” he added.

The study also showed that the royal family at times profited substantially from the colonial system, mostly from trade in the Dutch East Indies, modern-day Indonesia.

In the 19th century, for instance, profits accumulated to about $650m in modern terms, the researchers said.

On the other hand, the royal family earned “almost nothing” from the slave trade, the research showed.

The Dutch monarch, who in 2023 apologised for his ancestors’ lack of action against slavery, highlighted their lack of “counter-current leadership” in the face of colonialism.

The House of Orange has ruled the Netherlands since the late 16th century, first as “stadtholders” who presided over the republic, and later as the royal house when the Netherlands became a monarchy.

For most of this time, the Dutch ruled over vast colonies in Southeast Asia and the Caribbean, including what is now Indonesia and Suriname.

The findings could stir up the debate around reparations in the Netherlands. The Dutch government apologised in 2022 after acknowledging the Dutch state bore responsibility for transatlantic slavery. King Willem-Alexander apologised the following year.

The government at the time ruled out reparations, instead creating a 200 million euro ($238m) fund for social initiatives, which anti-racism campaigners have dismissed as insufficient.

The National Institute for the Dutch Slavery Past and Heritage (NiNsee) lauded the king for commissioning the study but said it should lead to a next phase.

“Research impacts society when the new insights into the past contribute to awareness, dialogue, corrections and additions to our national history in the school curriculum and the conversation about responsibility and reparatory justice,” NiNsee director Bianca Groen Gallant said.

The Dutch played a major role in the global slave trade from the 17th century until the Netherlands abolished slavery in the second half of the 19th century.

title: Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year?
excerpt:
For the first time in more than 30 years, a hurricane has not formed in the Atlantic throughout September - normally the most active month for hurricane activity.

The eerily quiet season continues an...
body_text:
For the first time in more than 30 years, a hurricane has not formed in the Atlantic throughout September - normally the most active month for hurricane activity.

The eerily quiet season continues and with just two months left, there is an increasing possibility that no hurricanes will develop at all.

This would make the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season the only one in the satellite era without a hurricane.

The biggest reason for this is El Niño, which traditionally stifles activity in the Atlantic but brings a very active season in the eastern North Pacific.

The Atlantic hurricane season was predicted to be quieter than normal as a result of this.

With a very strong El Niño forecast, the US National Hurricane Center in May predicted a total of eight to 14 named storms. Of those, three to six were predicted to become hurricanes, with one to three becoming major hurricanes.

September is typically the most active month for tropical storm and hurricane activity.

But, this year marks the latest date on record since the start of the satellite era (1960s onward) where no hurricane has formed in the North Atlantic.

While there have been no hurricanes forming in the North Atlantic so far this season, the Eastern North Pacific has been very active with above-average storms

There were, however, four named tropical storms which formed in September: Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo and Hanna.

All but Edouard stayed out in the open waters of the Atlantic.

The National Hurricane Center suggests there is no sign of any tropical storm activity or hurricane over the next week at least.

Forecasters at Colorado State University, who also monitor activity, suggest the strong El Niño is likely to disrupt wind patterns across the Atlantic and "likely result in below-normal activity" over the next two-weeks.

As the typical peak of the season has passed and is now on a downward trend until 30 November, a season without a single hurricane is looking increasingly possible.

In the historical Atlantic hurricane database,  there has not been a year without a hurricane recorded since 1914. However, this was pre-satellite monitoring so it is impossible to say with certainty that none formed.

While El Niño is the natural warming of the tropical Pacific, it can disrupt weather patterns around the globe.

As wind patterns shift during an El Niño, upper winds over the Atlantic increase and this leads to more wind shear, where wind changes rapidly with height.

Increased wind shear rips apart thunderstorms, preventing them from growing into tropical storms or hurricanes.

Meanwhile, the Pacific typically becomes more active during El Niño because the sea surface temperatures here are much higher, combined with more favourable wind patterns.

The warmer waters give storms more energy to grow into tropical storms and hurricanes.

This year, temperature records have already been broken in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific, with daily sea surface temperatures now exceeding the previous record set during the very strong El Niño of 2015.

There have so far been 17 named storms in the basin including nine hurricanes, seven of which were major.

In terms of the amount of energy these storms have produced - known as the Accumulated Cyclone Energy - this season is around two and half times more active than normal at this point.

El Niño is predicted to continue to strengthen with forecasts suggesting it will reach its peak in November or December.

title: Federal judge halts Big Bend border wall construction in blow to Trump agenda
excerpt:
Plan to install barriers through popular national park sparked outrage from advocates and politicians alike

A federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from expanding the border ...
body_text:
Plan to install barriers through popular national park sparked outrage from advocates and politicians alike

A federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from expanding the border wall and other security infrastructure across the Big Bend region of west Texas, where contentious plans to build roads and vehicle barriers through a popular national park have led to furious backlash and public protests.

US district judge Kathleen Cardone’s ruling after a Friday hearing in El Paso deals a major blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to expand the border wall through west Texas at breakneck pace, while riding roughshod over the objections of local business owners, landowners, public land advocates and politicians from both parties.

Plans to mar Big Bend national park with new roads and 6-ft tall vehicle barriers have drawn the most national attention since the Trump administration started advancing the border wall construction earlier this year. Images of bulldozers plowing up ground for new roads at the park in August drew outrage, prompting Rodney Scott, the CBP commissioner, to temporarily halt construction. Construction resumed in September.

Friday’s ruling came after a hearing in a lawsuit filed by the Friends of the Ruidosa church, the Center for Biological Diversity and river guide Billy Miller seeking to overturn several Department of Homeland Security (DHS) waivers that suspended dozens of environmental and historical protection laws to speed construction.

Cardone blocked the DHS waivers in her ruling, saying that the plaintiffs were likely to win and would suffer irreparable harm if construction moved forward. The ruling bars CBP from border security infrastructure construction or ground disturbance, unless it complies with the federal laws that DHS tried to suspend.

“This is a historic victory for Big Bend and everyone who loves this wild corner of Texas,” said Laiken Jordahl, a public land advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. “No administration has the right to destroy a crown-jewel national park for political theatre.”

“But this fight is far from over,” he added. “We won’t rest until Big Bend’s environmental protections are fully restored and the illegal waiver that allowed so much destruction is gone for good.”

CBP has already awarded five contracts for Big Bend totaling more than $6bn to expand what the agency calls the “smart wall” – a mix of 30-ft steel bollard fencing, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology.

“We stand by our assessment and remain confident in our legal authorities to secure the border while preserving the unique landscape of the Big Bend region,” a CBP spokesperson wrote in an email in response to the ruling. “We are working with the Department of Justice on next steps.”

The Republican-dominated Congress included a whopping $46.5bn for border wall construction in last year’s “big, beautiful” spending bill. That massive war chest led CBP to focus much of its efforts on the Big Bend region, which contains the longest unwalled stretch along the US-Mexico border.

The plans have sparked furious responses from landowners and local political leaders, who say that unauthorized crossings are already rare there due to the region’s remoteness, the lack of nearby cities on the Mexican side and prominent cliffs that make it very difficult to cross through many stretches of the border there.

title: Women given shorts at Oktoberfest to prevent upskirting
excerpt:
The famous Teufelsrad, or Devil's Wheel, from which videos are regularly posted online (file picture)

The operator of a popular amusement ride at the Munich Oktoberfest has been handing out free cycl...
body_text:
The famous Teufelsrad, or Devil's Wheel, from which videos are regularly posted online (file picture)

The operator of a popular amusement ride at the Munich Oktoberfest has been handing out free cycling shorts to women, after thousands of voyeuristic videos emerged on social media.

Some videos showing women on the Teufelsrad, or Devil's Wheel, have been viewed millions of times. One is said to have made thousands of euros for a woman who posted it online.

The Teufelsrad is one of the oldest attractions at the Oktoberfest, the annual beer festival which comes to an end this weekend after 16 days. Its circular platform rotates faster and faster until its riders fall off, and the motion and speed often make skirts fly up.

Filming under skirts is illegal in Germany, and carries a two-year sentence in jail.

However, critics believe the law does not go far enough, and the videos of women on the Teufelsrad in their traditional dirndl dresses often show their underwear. Sometimes, the images have been digitally altered to show them naked, according to local broadcaster BR.

Elisabeth Polaczy says she has handed out more than 100 pairs of cycle shorts this year

One woman made €9,000 (£7,650) from a single clip, according to BR, whose investigations found that a group of professional YouTubers from Ukraine and several people from Bavaria were behind the videos.

At least 32,000 videos of women on the Teufelsrad have been in circulation, according to Munich-based daily Süddeutsche Zeitung. Some have apparently been viewed millions of times.

The operator of the Teufelsrad, Elisabeth Polaczy, told the BBC that, for the past three years, she has been handing out free cycling shorts to women and girls wearing dresses, to protect them from people filming in the crowd.

This Oktoberfest she has handed out more than 100 pairs, she says: "I want to do everything I can to make people feel secure."

Polaczy, who is now 80, said donating cycling shorts wasn't cheap, but it was worth it for her own peace of mind.

The Teufelsrad tent is hung with signs and police posters in German and English warning against filming under people's skirts, but Polaczy says it is impossible to control everyone filming with smart phones.

Some waitresses at this year's beer festival say they have also started wearing cycling shorts under their dirndls.

A spokesman for the Bavarian police told the BBC that since 2025, it has run a poster campaign at the Oktoberfest, warning against upskirting.

A police poster in Munich timed for this year's Oktoberfest makes clear that "upskirting is a crime"

This year, police arrested a 45-year-old Swiss man for using his phone to film under a German woman's dirndl. Last year there were 10 arrests for upskirting and seven in 2024.

However, Josephine Ballon, who heads German non-profit organisation Hate Aid,  which aims to support victims of digital violence, told the BBC that the current law against upskirting does not provide enough protection.

Although she says there are plans for a new law, current legislation "applies only when you film under the skirt", and not when a skirt simply flies up and gets photographed.

The new camera glasses are also a threat, she believes.

Ballon wants anyone who has uploaded intimate pictures of women on the internet to be punished, along with the platforms that put them up.

Meanwhile, the city of Munich has sought to tighten up on influencers and content creators who earn money from their social media postings and who want to film at the Oktoberfest.

Munich has banned broadcasting live streams from the festival and requires anyone who wants to film there to hold a permit, which is issued by the city for a fee.

Hundreds of licences have been issued this year to influencers, who make money from product placement or sponsoring.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Michael McDonald’s long-lost son reveals stunning moment he discovered famous father after 58 years
excerpt:
Michael Goessling tells Fox News Digital how a mysterious call with a musician named ‘Mike’ led to an unbelievable realization with a quick internet search.

EXCLUSIVE: Michael Goessling always knew h...
body_text:
Michael Goessling tells Fox News Digital how a mysterious call with a musician named ‘Mike’ led to an unbelievable realization with a quick internet search.

EXCLUSIVE: Michael Goessling always knew he was adopted. But what he did not know for nearly 58 years was that his biological father had one of the most recognizable and beloved voices in American music.

The St. Louis man learned recently that his father was five-time Grammy winner and Doobie Brothers singer Michael McDonald, a musician Goessling had admired since childhood and had unknowingly paid to see perform twice as a young man.

But even after receiving the letter that began it all, meeting his biological mother and learning his biological father was a mysterious musician named "Mike," Goessling still had no idea who was waiting on the other end of the phone.

RITA WILSON LEARNED ABOUT FATHER’S TRAGIC PAST, SECRET FAMILY IN BULGARIA ON TV SHOW

Michael Goessling, right, spoke with Fox News Digital about discovering at 58 that Michael McDonald was his biological father. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)

The answer finally came during their first conversation, when "Mike" mentioned he was touring and would be stopping in St. Louis on Sept. 4 at a venue he believed was called "Hollywood."

Goessling thought of the Hollywood Casino Amphitheater and, puzzled that his biological father was apparently still a touring musician at his age, began searching the venue's concert schedule as the two men spoke.

The Doobie Brothers were playing in concert Sept. 4.

Suddenly, the pieces began falling into place: "Mike." Musician. That unmistakable voice.

"Are you Michael McDonald?" Goessling finally asked.

"Oh my gosh, this is getting crazier by the second," Goessling recalled saying. "I can't even, I can't get my head around this. This is too much."

"I know," McDonald replied. "Take a minute."

"I thought I was being punked for a second," Goessling told Fox News Digital. "It's like, no, this can't be real. This is impossible. What is going on here?"

More than a year later, he said the discovery can still feel unreal.

NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS

Michael Goessling credits his adoptive parents, Paul and Kay Goessling, with giving him a "charmed" childhood. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)

"I still wake up sometimes and my first thought is, ‘Oh my gosh, that was a crazy dream,’ only to realize that here we are."

The extraordinary phone call came just days after a letter ended a mystery stretching back to Goessling's birth. On May 6, 2025, an attorney representing his biological mother contacted Goessling to explain that she believed he was the son she had placed for adoption through Catholic Charities nearly 58 years earlier.

Goessling had always known he was adopted, but the adoption was closed. He knew nothing about his biological parents, and they knew virtually nothing about the life he had gone on to live.

His biological mother, he learned, had spent roughly 30 to 35 years searching for him. Both biological parents hoped he might be willing to communicate, Goessling recalled, but above all, they wanted to know that he was well.

"It was a wonderful surprise, but quite a shock," he said. "It felt like a tsunami hit me."

Goessling called his biological mother that evening. Although he had never actively searched for his biological parents, he had long hoped he might someday have the opportunity to thank them.

"I just want you to hear from me that I got nothing but love for you," he recalled telling her. "This is such an amazing gift, that I get to thank you personally … They were always heroes in my story," he said.

CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT

Michael Goessling said people compared his appearance to Michael McDonald years before he discovered the singer was his biological father. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)

Their first conversation lasted about 90 minutes. Goessling eventually proposed meeting for lunch that Friday, prompting his biological mother to remind him that Friday was his birthday.

"Yeah, yeah. You've waited long enough. I think I've waited enough," he recalled replying. "Let's meet on my birthday, 58 years to the day."

After a three-hour lunch and nearly six decades apart, Goessling learned there was someone else anxious to speak with him. His biological father had deliberately remained in the background so mother and son could have their reunion first.

"He really wanted the mother-son thing to happen first, which is just true to his character," Goessling said. "He thought that was very important, and he wanted to take a back seat so that could happen."

Before father and son connected, McDonald left Goessling a voicemail. That unmistakable voice immediately struck him.

"Whoa, what a voice," Goessling recalled telling his biological mother.

"Yeah, he gets that a lot," she replied with a chuckle.

The voice seemed strangely familiar, but Goessling still didn't make the connection. When the two men finally spoke, he began by telling McDonald what he had already told his biological mother.

"Thank you for giving me a shot in this world," Goessling recalled saying. "I've had a charmed life. And it all started with you guys."

Then he asked what his biological father did for a living.

Goessling, a lifelong music obsessive who once worked in the music business, thought that was terrific. It wasn't until the conversation turned to McDonald's upcoming tour stop that he finally put it together.

The revelation contained another coincidence almost too remarkable to invent; Goessling was already a huge fan.

The Doobie Brothers had been among his favorite bands since childhood, alongside The Who and Journey. He vividly remembers first hearing "Takin' It to the Streets" after McDonald joined the group and insisting to the person playing it that there had been some mistake.

"I know the Doobie Brothers and that is not the Doobie Brothers," Goessling remembered declaring as a child.

He soon learned about the band's new singer and became a McDonald fan, too. He stayed one.

In fact, Goessling had already watched his biological father perform in concert twice, once in the 1980s, and again in the early 1990s, without ever imagining that the man onstage was the father whose identity he did not know.

When Fox News Digital pointed out that meant he had actually paid twice to see his own father perform, Goessling laughed.

There were other clues hiding in plain sight. After Goessling grew out his hair and white beard during the COVID-19 pandemic, people began telling him they liked the "Michael McDonald thing" he had going on.

"Little did I know five years later that that would resonate even so true," he said.

After the families met, the similarities became even harder to miss. During a visit with McDonald, Goessling said McDonald's wife, Amy, and his newfound half-sister would watch him do or say something and suddenly burst out laughing.

Michael McDonald, of the Doobie Brothers, poses for a portrait at Show Biz Studios in Los Angeles on Aug. 17, 2021. McDonald has a new memoir titled, "What a Fool Believes."  (Chris Pizzello/AP Photo, File)

"Your dad does the exact same thing," they would tell him. "They couldn't take their eyes off me," Goessling said. "They're waiting to see what I would do or say next because there was so many just natural similarities."

Yet for Goessling, the remarkable celebrity connection is not the part of his story that matters most.

Learning where he came from also meant finally understanding what his biological parents had faced nearly six decades earlier, when they were just two 14-year-old eighth-graders confronting a pregnancy that would change all three of their lives.

According to Goessling, the teenagers' initial reaction was that they would marry, raise their baby and rely on their families to help them. Their parents concluded they were simply too young at the time.

"They were just far too young to be married and to have a child," Goessling said.

Their families ultimately determined that adoption would be best, he said, although relinquishing their son had not been his biological parents' first choice.

Nearly six decades later, Goessling sees what happened through the lens of both gratitude and faith.

"Mike, I mean, he wasn't Michael McDonald [then]. He was Mike from the neighborhood," he said, imagining how differently life could have been had two 14-year-olds attempted to raise a child together.

Patrick Simmons, left, Tom Johnston, John McFee, Marc Russo, Michael McDonald, and Ed Toth of The Doobie Brothers perform onstage in Pacific Palisades, Calif. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for BC, File)

"I have to believe that it all worked out as it was supposed to because certainly when I see us all now together, it's just the greatest joy," Goessling said. "I think this was the plan. And I think it was a beautiful plan."

That plan, as Goessling sees it, led him to Paul and Kay Goessling. He grew up in a family of four children. Three were adopted before, against the odds, Kay became pregnant with their youngest daughter, Linda.

Goessling describes his childhood as "charmed" and said he could not have chosen better parents himself.

"If I could go back and pick two folks, I would pick them and do it all over again," he said. "They were just the most wonderful blessing in my life."

His father, Paul, died shortly before Christmas 2024 after a long battle with Parkinson's disease and Goessling said the two were extremely close. Six months later, another father entered his life.

"After losing my father, I get a letter and Mike pops up," Goessling said. "Another father enters my life, my world."

Kay's reaction to the discovery was immediate. When Goessling showed her the letter, he said his mother began crying and declared what had happened "a miracle."

She asked whether he had met his biological mother, and he had.

"Oh my God, go get her," Goessling recalled Kay saying. "I have to meet her. I've got a million questions. What's she like? I gotta give her a big hug."

Goessling said his mother has embraced his biological family from the beginning, and the once-separate branches of his family came together with surprising ease.

"Everybody's in love with everybody," he said.

Michael McDonald performs the national anthem before a Los Angeles Lakers game at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles.  (Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images, File)

Father and son now speak frequently and text "all the time," according to Goessling.

And while the identity of his biological father is what thrust his story into the spotlight, Goessling hopes the attention gives him an opportunity to talk about adoption as a blessing.

A practicing Catholic who was raised in the faith and adopted through Catholic Charities, Goessling said his parents taught him from childhood to understand his adoption not as evidence that he had been unwanted, but as evidence that he was deeply loved.

Even before he was old enough to fully understand what adoption meant, he knew how his parents viewed it.

"It was a miracle," he said. "It was the greatest thing. It was a gift from God."

Only when Goessling grew old enough to understand where babies came from, he said, did he fully appreciate the significance of the decisions that had been made before his birth.

"Obviously, we all know there are choices in this world, and I am so grateful and fortunate for the choices they made on my behalf," he said. "Adoption has been absolutely nothing but a blessing for me … I celebrate adoption and I always have. It's always been a big part of my life story."

Now, nearly six decades later, Goessling has been able to thank the biological parents he once could only imagine, and discovered that they had spent those same decades wondering about him.

He hopes the unlikely circumstances that brought attention to his family can help "elevate" the conversation surrounding adoption.

"I want this to elevate the narrative, the adoption narrative," he said. "I want that adoption gets celebrated more in this country. If my crazy story can be true, Lord knows anything is possible."

And if Michael McDonald is watching? Goessling doesn't need an interview to deliver the message. He said father and son already talk regularly.

"I just tell him that I love him and I tell him thank you for everything," he said.

After 58 years, the man who says he never felt deprived of a family has somehow ended up with an even larger one.

Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: The vanishing world of India's street magicians
excerpt:
Ishamuddin Khan is one of India's most famous street magicians

Sitting in his cramped Delhi home, Ishamuddin Khan can still make a rope appear to rise into the air.

The 55-year-old magician spent de...
body_text:
Ishamuddin Khan is one of India's most famous street magicians

Sitting in his cramped Delhi home, Ishamuddin Khan can still make a rope appear to rise into the air.

The 55-year-old magician spent decades performing a trick once dismissed as legend, and still keeps photographs and newspaper clippings from his years of international fame.

These days, he spends more time looking back at those memories than performing the trick.

"The times have changed," he says.  "Street magic is dying a slow death. It is on a ventilator."

Khan's story reflects a wider change in India, where traditional street performers are finding it increasingly difficult to make a living from their craft.

Magicians, jugglers, puppeteers and acrobats once made a living from crowds in public spaces. Changing entertainment habits and tighter restrictions have made audiences harder to find, pushing many out of the profession.

Khan, one of India's best-known magicians, comes from the Madari community, which has a long tradition of performing in public spaces.

There are no official figures, but Khan says community records identify about 400 Madari families in Delhi, with hundreds more in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Telangana.

Despite their small numbers today, the Madaris trace their roots back centuries.

Historian Ashok Mathur says Madari traditions have roots in Indian folklore, mythology and the long history of travelling performers.

"For generations, these skills were passed through families," he explains.

Restricted access to community spaces has made it difficult for street magicians to find an audience

Khan followed the same path, learning magic from his father and uncles and performing from the age of 12. By his early 20s, he had mastered the rope trick that would later make him famous.

The trick – in which a rope appears to rise into the air before a boy climbs it – was long associated with the mythology of Indian street magic and widely considered impossible, until Khan performed it.

He says it took six years to master the trick, which he first performed publicly in 1995 outside Delhi's iconic Qutub Minar. Two years later, he performed it before 30,000 people on a beach in Karnataka.

His trick brought international attention,  and that led to tours to the UK, France, Germany and Japan.

Khan hoped the fame would shine a light on India's traditional performers. For a while, it did. But the attention faded.

As audiences turned to new forms of entertainment and public performance opportunities dwindled, many magicians found it harder to make a living from skills passed down through generations.

Once a magician, Imam now makes a living collecting bottles and recyclables from Delhi's streets. He spends much of his time rag-picking near a western Delhi dump, earning about 200 rupees ($2; £1.57) a day.

Experts say the decline in street performance has multiple causes, chief among them the changing nature of public spaces.

An old picture of Khan performing the great rope trick

Anurupa Roy, founder of Katkatha Puppet Arts Trust, says performers increasingly struggle to find audiences as public spaces shrink.

"Closed parks and residential societies that bar outsiders are limiting spaces for performance."

Researcher and performer Komita Dhanda says changing attitudes to public spaces are also driving the decline.

"With tighter security, especially in busy town and city centres, there is little space left for street performers," she says.

It is not just individual artists who struggle to get permission. Dhanda says her well-known street theatre group, Jana Natya Manch, often faces hurdles performing in public spaces.

For many artists, the challenge is not just finding a venue but navigating unclear rules over what is allowed.

Most street performers rely on voluntary payments, but experts say the line between performing for money and begging can blur.

Unlike the UK, India has no federal busking framework. Performers instead navigate state-level rules on public order, obstruction, noise and public land.

"This is why street performers often have to face municipal and police regulations governing public spaces, as well as state-specific anti-begging laws," says lawyer Kaushik Mitra.

Imam Khan has left street performance behind and now makes a living as a ragpicker

For many artists, Covid made a bad situation worse.

When India imposed its 2020 lockdown, public performances stopped. Many magicians returned to their villages; some never came back.

"We saw a decline in public performances after this period," Dhanda says. "The brunt was especially harsh for street magicians and performers, many of whom did not return to cities."

For the artists who did return and continue the trade, the challenges only increased.

Shahim Khan, 42, still performs magic on Delhi's streets, sometimes with his 12-year-old daughter, Alia.

Much of his work is now confined to industrial areas, far from the busy public spaces where he once performed, hitting his earnings hard.

Before the pandemic, he could stage four or five shows a day, earning 1,000-1,200 rupees.

"Now I barely manage two shows and earn 200-400 rupees," he says.

The rise of short-form digital entertainment has added to the pressures on traditional performers, experts say. So have changing attitudes towards street arts.

"There was a lot of Western interest in things like the rope trick decades ago. But forms and tastes have changed, and so has what India chooses to showcase," Dhanda says.

For Khan, the loss is about more than money. He fears an art passed down generations could disappear if no-one learns it.

"A trick can survive only if someone learns it," he says.

His son, Altamash, began performing with him as a teenager but now works decorating parties with balloons. In his 30s, he has largely left performing behind.

Years without regular practice have dulled his skills. When he demonstrated his juggling for the BBC, he struggled to find the rhythm.

"I am slowly forgetting all the tricks," he said.

Khan had hoped his son would carry on the family tradition. Altamash had hoped to make a name for himself too, but it did not work out.

"I knew I may not achieve the fame my father has, but I did not think there would come a time when performing would not remain an option," he says.

The 'maharajah of magic' who terrified the UK

title: Flydubai pilot recounts cockpit stabbing in call with Indian PM Modi
excerpt: Indian pilot Smit Machchhar, who was stabbed by his co-pilot in an alleged attempt to crash a Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv, has shared a public account of how he managed to open the cockpit door and le...
body_text:
Indian pilot Smit Machchhar, who was stabbed by his co-pilot in an alleged attempt to crash a Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv, has shared a public account of how he managed to open the cockpit door and let passengers take control of the plane despite his injuries.

Speaking on Friday from a hospital bed in Abu Dhabi via video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Machchhar said that he knew the aircraft was going down as he lay bleeding on the floor.

“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push, that the door was right there,” he said in a nearly 10-minute video released on the prime minister’s social media channels.

He added: “I was being hit even then, but I just opened the door and everyone came in.”

Machchhar, who has 17 years of aviation experience, including 11 as a captain, said that experience helped him grasp what was happening even while wounded.

He told Modi he had recited a Hindu devotional prayer during the ordeal.

“I know God himself saved me,” he said, in an emotional exchange with Modi, who is from the same home state of Gujarat.

Modi praised Machchhar’s bravery, saying his presence of mind had saved lives and the reputation of Indian pilots.

Machchhar said he allowed passengers and crew to overpower the co-pilot and let a second pair of Flydubai pilots take control and land the plane in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

The Flydubai flight was carrying 174 people as it briefly plunged around 17,000 feet (5,180 metres) before it was brought back under control.

UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash has called the incident a “terrorist act”, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination” and appeared “suicidal”.

US President Donald Trump has warned that Iran would be “hit very hard” if found to be linked to the attack.

The United Arab Emirates has said it will launch an investigation into the incident.

title: DoJ declines to reopen investigation into former Fed chair Jay Powell
excerpt:
Kevin Warsh’s predecessor had been investigated over cost overruns related to central bank renovation project

The US ⁠justice department is not reopening a criminal investigation into former Federal ...
body_text:
Kevin Warsh’s predecessor had been investigated over cost overruns related to central bank renovation project

The US ⁠justice department is not reopening a criminal investigation into former Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell ⁠for cost overruns ⁠related ​to the central bank’s building renovation project, a department spokesperson said on Friday.

Attorney general Todd ⁠Blanche – in comments to Bloomberg News, which first reported the development – said he has not ruled out ⁠continuing to look into the project’s oversight and potentially take ​action if evidence of ‌wrongdoing came to ‌light.

The Fed’s inspector general on Wednesday said it found ‌no grounds for a criminal referral or evidence of administrative misconduct tied to the project cost overruns. But its conclusion there was lax oversight drew a fresh call for Powell’s resignation from Donald Trump, who across his two presidencies has been a vociferous critic of Powell.

Powell has remained at ‌the Fed as a governor since stepping down as chair in May.

His successor as Fed chair, Kevin ​Warsh said, on Thursday he would hire an independent auditor to “verify accuracy and compliance” for all of the project’s costs.

Blanche told Bloomberg News that if the new review found any evidence ⁠of criminal wrongdoing, the justice department could investigate.

At his final ​press conference ​as Fed chief in ​April, Powell said he would not leave the ​central bank’s board “until this ‌investigation is well and ​truly over, ​with transparency and finality”.

A Fed spokesperson had no immediate comment on Blanche’s statements.

title: Christa Pike remains on ventilator after failed execution in Tennessee
excerpt:
Attorneys say hospital staff are working to clear pentobarbital she was administered from her system

Christa Pike remained hospitalized, unconscious and on a machine helping her breathe after her fai...
body_text:
Attorneys say hospital staff are working to clear pentobarbital she was administered from her system

Christa Pike remained hospitalized, unconscious and on a machine helping her breathe after her failed execution in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday.

The attorneys said hospital staff were working to save Pike’s life and clear the pentobarbital she was administered from her system as of late Thursday.

Pike received two doses of the drug in a failed attempt by the state of Tennessee to execute her on Wednesday.

In the court filing, Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with intravenous lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.

“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike’s body,” they wrote.

They also wrote that instead of “remedying this failure” the execution team proceeded to prepare and administer a backup set of pentobarbital syringes.

In a statement reported on X by NewsNation journalist Brian Entin, Pike’s attorneys described her as “critically ill and … receiving medical care for the devastating effects of Wednesday nights events”.

“We are working close with those closest to Christa to respect her wishes, safeguard her privacy and protect her rights as a patient during this extraordinarily difficult time,” the statement also said. “We ask that the public and the media respect that privacy as well.”

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 at the age of 20 in connection with the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike and her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, killed Slemmer at a job training camp in Knoxville, Tennessee.

One grim detail about the case is that a satanic symbol had been carved into Slemmer’s chest.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the last execution of a woman in Tennessee was in 1820, meaning Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in more than 200 years.

Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Pike has prompted top lawyers, doctors and members of the faith community to call for a moratorium on the death penalty in the US.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Magnitude 4.8 earthquake hits Victoria with tremors felt across Melbourne
excerpt:
The epicentre was at Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with residents reporting houses shaking just after 2am

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A magnitude 4.8 eart...
body_text:
The epicentre was at Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with residents reporting houses shaking just after 2am

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A magnitude 4.8 earthquake struck Victoria in the early hours of Saturday morning, shaking Melbourne and waking people across the whole region.

Geoscience Australia said it detected an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 4.8 at 2.01am near Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with the tremors felt across the city’s eastern suburbs.

Geoscience Australia said it had received thousands of reports from people who said they had felt the earthquake.

Posting on Facebook, Brian Morley in Narre Warren said “felt it and woke me up”, while Theresa Stevens said: “Shook our house in Garfield.”

Other posts indicated the quake had been felt in Preston, Heidelberg Heights, Venus Bay and many other parts of Melbourne.

The quake was estimated to have struck at about 10km below the Earth’s surface.

Victoria’s State Emergency Service said the earthquake was a “timely reminder” to remember the drill to follow during an earthquake and that was drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy piece of furniture and protect your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops.

The Bureau of Meteorology said there was no tsunami threat from the quake.

title: Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s partner, Ken Urker, found dead inside his Louisiana home: sheriff
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office confirmed Kenan "Ken" Urker, the partner of Gypsy Rose Blanchard, was found dead...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office confirmed Kenan "Ken" Urker, the partner of Gypsy Rose Blanchard, was found dead inside his Louisiana home Thursday after loved ones requested a welfare check.

Anita Blanchard told authorities that she and her husband, who is Gypsy Rose Blanchard's half-brother, went to the 34-year-old's home and spotted Urker lying unconscious from an outside window, according to an incident report.

A man accompanying Anita Blanchard and her husband then entered the house through a window and found Urker, who was not breathing and cold to the touch, according to the report.

GYPSY ROSE BLANCHARD IS ENGAGED TO MAN WHO CONTACTED HER IN PRISON, REPORT SAYS

Gypsy Rose Blanchard attends "The Prison Confessions of Gypsy Rose Blanchard" red carpet event on Jan. 5, 2024, in New York City. On Thursday, authorities found Blacnchard's partner, Kenan "Ken" Urker, dead in his Louisiana home. (Getty Images)

Investigators recovered syringes and a spoon next to a brown powdery substance in the bathroom, as well as a handgun, two shot glasses, and a syringe on a nightstand next to the bed, the report states.

Deputies noted Urker "appeared to have been there for an extended period of time."

Anita Blanchard told authorities that Urker had been with her and her husband at church the previous evening around 8:45 p.m., where he mentioned feeling depressed and upset.

GYPSY ROSE BLANCHARD SAYS SHE 'FELT LIKE A PRISONER' BEFORE MOTHER'S FATAL STABBING

"They advised he made a TikTok live video at approximately 2300 hours," deputies wrote. "They advised that he just had the video going while he was driving without him saying anything."

Urker had amassed more than 36,000 followers on the platform.

After Urker failed to show up for work the following day, Anita Blanchard and Urker's employer decided to check on him, ultimately prompting them to contact law enforcement.

The sheriff's office told Fox News Digital the case remains under investigation, but there are "no signs of foul play." Thursday was Urker's 34th birthday.

"If that would change at any point, or there would be any major update in this investigation, we would issue a new statement," the sheriff's office said.

Gypsy Rose Blanchard and Melissa G. Moore attend An Evening with Lifetime: Conversations on Controversies FYC event at The Lounge at Studio 10 on May 1, 2024, in Los Angeles, Calif. (Variety via Getty Images)

HAYDEN PANETTIERE CAUSE OF DEATH REVEALED

Gypsy Rose Blanchard was sentenced to 10 years in prison for second-degree murder in 2016 for her role in the fatal stabbing of her mother, Clauddine "Dee Dee" Blanchard, alongside her then-boyfriend Nicholas Godejohn. The killing inspired the 2019 TV series "The Act" on Hulu.

Godejohn was sentenced to life in prison without parole. Blanchard was released on parole in December 2023 after serving 85% of her sentence.

Urker and Gypsy Rose Blanchard got engaged in 2018 while she was incarcerated, but later separated. The couple rekindled after her first marriage and welcomed their daughter, Aurora, on Dec. 28, 2024.

In a statement to PEOPLE, Blanchard said she believes Urker died of a drug overdose.

"I don’t know if it was intentional or not," Gypsy Rose Blanchard told the outlet. "He was not in a good state of mind lately."

She shared a photo of Urker on Instagram Friday, writing, "You will always be my greatest love story. You will be remembered and loved forever."

Gypsy Rose Blanchard also shared an Instagram Story detailing his struggle with cyberbullying.

"Ken endured an unimaginable level of public scrutiny and relentless cyberbullying across social media platforms, including TikTok and Reddit," she wrote. "The cruelty directed toward him was something no human being should have to endure. I believe the tremendous weight of that scrutiny and harassment had a profound impact on him, and I hope his passing serves as a reminder that there is a real person behind every screen, every headline, and every comment."

"I will make sure [Aurora] grows up knowing how deeply her father loved her and who he was beyond what strangers on the internet chose to say about him," she added.

The post, shared with her one million followers, garnered nearly 100,000 likes within hours.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Two Iranian men charged over alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community
excerpt:
The men were arrested on 20 September, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar

Two Iranian men have been charged in relation to an alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s ...
body_text:
The men were arrested on 20 September, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar

Two Iranian men have been charged in relation to an alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community.

Rahman Salehi, 35, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, have been charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism.

Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism police (CTP), said: “These are extremely serious charges and allegations, and have come about from a joint CTP investigation, working closely with our partners in the security services. This investigation has led to the disruption of what we believe to have been a plot targeting the Jewish community in Manchester.”

She added: “This week also brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran. While this incident and the investigation into the RAF Fairford incident are not connected in any way, I want to reassure the public that CTP, working with our national security partners, are using the full range of our capabilities to protect the UK from any hostile acts.”

The men, both in their 30s, were arrested on 20 September, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

They were arrested in ​Newton Street, in the Northern Quarter area of the city centre, before being held in custody at a London police station.

Counter-terrorism police had been given more time to question the men, who were detained under section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said: “These recent events are a stark reminder of the threats posed against this country from both terrorists and foreign state actors.

“This news will be deeply distressing for our Jewish communities, coming so soon after Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. I know this will be especially true in Manchester, as we mark one year since the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue.

“The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country. While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do.”

Salehi and Ahmadyan They are due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 3 October.

Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “We have decided to prosecute Rahman Salehi and Salam Ahmadyan following a fast-paced counter-terrorism policing investigation in Greater Manchester in September targeting the Jewish community.

“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and we remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendants in this case are active and they have the right to a fair trial.

“We understand that this case may cause concern, particularly considering the arrests came on the eve of Yom Kippur. We want to assure the Jewish community that working with the police, their safety and that of the wider public is our highest priority.”

The Metropolitan police, who are leading the investigation, said searches had also been carried out at properties on Epworth Street in Liverpool and Lancaster Road in Salford.

At the time of the arrests, Evans said police officers were “doing everything we can to keep them [the Jewish community] and the wider public safe”, while counter-terrorism police and local forces were working together “to provide protective security support and advice for areas with Jewish communities, and particularly during the High Holy Day period”.

Last year, Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, was shot dead by armed police after launching a terror attack during Yom Kippur at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester.

Two men were killed during the attack, Adrian Daulby, 53, and Melvin Cravitz, 66, while three others were injured.

title: Social media reacts to excruciatingly awkward moment between Devils Jack Hughes and ESPN analyst
excerpt: Cal and Jody hear from a caller wanting to talk about the Chicago Bears. That’s as normal as sports radio gets, until it starts to seem like this listener could be phoning in from across time and spac...
body_text:
Cal and Jody hear from a caller wanting to talk about the Chicago Bears. That’s as normal as sports radio gets, until it starts to seem like this listener could be phoning in from across time and space.

The NHL season is just a few days old, and it's safe to say that we have a frontrunner for "Awkward Moment of the Year" already.

This one comes courtesy of New Jersey Devils star Jack Hughes and ESPN analyst AJ Mleczko.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The Devils hosted the Philadelphia Flyers for their season opener at the Prudential Center. After the first period, the Devils were down 1-0, and Hughes was called over to do an interview with Mleczko, who was stationed between the benches.

AVALANCHE FORWARD NATHAN MACKINNON SCORES A PAIR THEN DROPS GLOVES, MIGHT BE THE BEST PLAYER IN THE WORLD

New Jersey Devils star Jack Hughes had an awkward moment with ESPN's AJ Mleczko. (Photo by Rich Graessle/NHLI via Getty Images)

Hughes offered the usual interview platitudes and seemed to be pleased with how his team was playing.

But then Mleczko decided to make a joke about the Team USA golden goal scorer's injury history, including an infamous moment in which he sustained a cut during a team dinner.

WYNDHAM CLARK TROLLS CANADIAN OPEN CROWD WITH TEAM USA JACK HUGHES JERSEY, GETS SHOWERED WITH BOOS

How did it go? Well, about as well as a dog fart at a wake.

It's a rough one, and you've got a clear line of demarcation, with some going after Mleczko for making the joke.

Others said criticism of her was misogynistic or saw it as an opportunity to go after Hughes for laughing at a joke the president made after the gold medal game.

Personally, I think it was a perfect storm of awkwardness. Just an accidental mixing of social bleach and ammonia.

I think Mleczko is a really solid broadcaster, and everyone has moments where they say something they wish they could grab out of the air and pretend it never happened.

ESPN analyst and former Olympian AJ Mleczko had a joke fall flat on Thursday, and to make matters worse, she made it to the wrong player. (Photo by Bill Wippert/NHLI via Getty Images)

Any analyst who tried to make that joke would've ended up with egg on their face too.

Hughes is not known to be one of the more gregarious NHLers. If you make a joke like that, someone like the Flyers' Trevor Zegras or Florida's Brad Marchand would field it and probably volley one back in the other direction.

I think Mleczko's biggest mistake was taking the wrong approach with the wrong player.

American Women's Ice Hockey Gold Medalist A.J. Mleczko looks on during NHL Street Hockey on "The Today Show" at Rockefeller Center in New York City on Sept. 6, 2017. (NHLI via Getty Images)

But it is also weird to take an awkward moment, tie it back to an unrelated and overblown moment from months earlier, in a vain attempt to build a narrative that just doesn't seem to be there.

title: College football refs ruin another game, Paige Spiranac whips up some eggs & Tony Romo's next move
excerpt:
A'ja Wilson's mom reacts to question about what her "love beats hate" sign means after Las Vegas Aces defeated the Indiana Fever in the playoffs.

'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on ...
body_text:
A'ja Wilson's mom reacts to question about what her "love beats hate" sign means after Las Vegas Aces defeated the Indiana Fever in the playoffs.

'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

First Friday of October? Come on! Might be right up there with the best weekend of the year. Fall is in the air. The leaves are turning. The sun is setting just a tad earlier every night. The weather is crisping up nicely.

Unless, of course, you're down here in Florida. It's rained every single day this week. It's raining right now. It'll be raining later. It's horrible.

We actually lost power, briefly, during the Braves game earlier this week. My wife is a huge Braves fan. It was chaos. I thought we were all done for.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Luckily, it came back on a few minutes later. The Braves went on to win. And then they won again last night. That means it's gonna be a much better first October weekend in this house.

Officials review Tulsa's two-point conversion attempt to verify the call at the end of the North Texas vs. Tulsa football game at H.A. Chapman Stadium in Tulsa, Okla., on Oct. 1, 2026. (Ron Lane/Cal Sport Media/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)

Welcome to a Friday Nightcaps — the one where the college football refs ruined yet another game last night. Amazing.

What else? I've got Paige Spiranac whipping up some breakfast to get our weekend started with a bang, Lexie Hull getting tossed around like a ragdoll while the equally insufferable WNBA refs turned a blind eye and the Tony Romo era at CBS is officially donezo.

But have we heard that last from Tony? I doubt it. You'll see.

OK, grab you whatever you need to get you through the final few hours of this work day, and settle in for a first-Friday-of-October 'Cap!

This is gonna be a quick class, because it's a Friday and we have college football to bet on tonight.

How about Virginia Tech, by the way? The Hokies are 4-0 and now we're getting a meaningful night game in Blacksburg for the first time in what feels like a decade?

Goodness, how lucky are we? Pitt-Va. Tech. at 7 p.m., and we also get Northwestern christening their new stadium against Penn State at 8 p.m. over on Fox. Like I said yesterday — this is the best time of year.

Soak it all in, boys and girls. Don't waste a single second.

OK, now we're gonna start class with last night's debacle in Oklahoma, where Tulsa was screwed out of a game-winning two-point conversion ...

But they also shouldn't have been there in the first place:

In no world is that first "touchdown" a touchdown. It's just simply the incorrect call. I couldn't believe my eyes as I was watching it live. You can't step out and then touch the ball before reestablishing yourself. That's Football 101. It was clear as day, they reviewed it for 20 seconds, and then upheld the call.

Ridiculous. What are we doing here? There has to be some accountability. It's nonsense.

BREAKING UP TROY AIKMAN AND JOE BUCK WOULD BE A BIG MISTAKE FOR ESPN | BOBBY BURACK

As for the non-call in overtime ... that one is a little tougher for me. It's certainly not as clear as the first play.

This angle makes me think it was a conversion:

I don't see a knee on the ground. I don't see a shin on the ground. I don't see a cheek on the ground. I see the ball break the plane.

Again, that one's a tougher call because it's close. The call on the field worked against Tulsa, so I can see them upholding it. Don't agree with it, but I understand the logic behind it.

The first one, though? That's nasty work by the refs. Both teams deserved better last night.

And you know who else deserved better? Lexie Hull, who's spending her first day of the WNBA offseason in an ice bath:

Goodness gracious. Just a violent takedown. And, somehow, the foul is called on the player who is currently getting arm-barred into next week.

The entire sequence is just so perfect for the WNBA. It's everything right — and wrong — with that league.

The officiating is just horrible. That's No. 1. We forget about just how truly awful the officials are most of the year because there's so much other nonsense going on, but at the end of the day, they are undoubtedly the worst officials in all of sports.

And that includes the nonsense we saw in Tulsa last night!

Indiana Fever guard Lexie Hull reacts to a call Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, during the first half of Game 3 of the first round of the WNBA Playoffs at Michelob ULTRA Arena in Las Vegas. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Remember earlier this summer when Sophie Cunningham got her teeth cracked by an elbow and no foul was called? Amazing. Same thing here with Lexie Hull.

Good riddance, WNBA. No, the season isn't over. But nobody will watch or care anymore. Caitlin Clark is out. Sophie Cunningham is out. It's over.

Can't wait to see the girls lace 'em back up next May! All eyes on the draft.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Friday class into a big Friday night. First up? We've ripped college football and WNBA officials so far today ...

Might as well end it with the fellas in the NFL!

This isn't a great look for the "there's no Patrick Mahomes bias in the NFL!" crowd ...

Lordy. I knew it was bad when I watched it live last Sunday. I said as much in Monday's class. But I didn't realize it was that bad.

Next? On the way out, let's all say goodbye to Tony Romo ... for now:

I'll be the first to admit, I didn't think CBS would do it. When Romo got arrested last summer, I figured he'd be back in the booth in no time.

I believe I even said he'd be back before Game 1. I was wrong.

Things were very clearly bad behind the scenes. So bad, CBS basically bought him out and decided to eat the contract. I'm not a huge Romo fan. I think he's been pretty awful the past few years.

Jim Nantz and Tony Romo, CBS Sports, speak on stage during the New York Upfront Partnership Event 2026 at Storied NYC on April 23, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images)

That being said ... I'd be shocked if he doesn't land a pretty big gig next season. I have no clue where it'll be, but I wouldn't bet against him.

Maybe Netflix? They appear to be getting pretty serious about the NFL.

There's also something ... fishy ... going on with Troy Aikman and ESPN at the moment. Joe Buck just signed a massive contract extension with ESPN, but it's been all quiet on the Aikman front. Him and Buck have historically been a package deal.

Maybe it's nothing. But, maybe it's something worth watching.

OK, that's it for today — and this week. Happy first weekend of October, everyone. Let's go have a big one.

Thoughts on the Tulsa game? Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

title: Wynonna Judd calls out Rosie O’Donnell after political comments leave country star ‘in shock’
excerpt:

Wynonna Judd was caught off guard when she lear...
body_text:
Wynonna Judd told Fox News Digital, her and her mom Naomi Judd's shared love of music helped them "bypass the bullcrap" and build a close relationship.

Wynonna Judd was caught off guard when she learned what Rosie O’Donnell had been saying about her political beliefs.

The country music icon is pushing back after O'Donnell publicly described her as a supporter of President Donald Trump.

"I’m in shock, just so you know," Judd told People. "I’ve never spoken to her about politics in my life … She doesn’t know anything about my stuff. I’m an independent."

ROSIE O'DONNELL CLAIMS TRUMP HAS 'PTSD RESPONSE' TO HER AS BACKLASH ERUPTS

Wynonna Judd said she was "in shock" after Rosie O'Donnell described her as a supporter of President Donald Trump. (Erika Goldring, Paula Lobo / Getty Images; NBC via Getty Images Source: Getty Images, NBC)

"I don’t know where it came [from]. It’s complete assumption," she said. "I heard it and I went, ‘What the …?’ I don’t ever remember talking to her about this, so she’s just assuming.’"

"I’m not angry," she said, describing herself as confused by O’Donnell’s comments.

But Judd said there was never a political conversation for O’Donnell to draw that conclusion from.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Rosie O'Donnell and Wynonna Judd have maintained a friendship for decades. (Sylvain Gaboury / FilmMagic)

And she isn't interested in turning the misunderstanding into a celebrity political battle.

"I just don’t want drama," Judd said. "So, if there’s going to be drama [about it], I’m like, ‘Oh for crap’s sake, there’s so much going on right now in the world. Can we just love each other?’"

Fox News Digital has reached out to O’Donnell for comment.

Judd's comments come after O’Donnell discussed their friendship during an August appearance on "The Tangle with Kyle Ridley" podcast.

Wynonna Judd said Rosie O'Donnell made a "complete assumption" about her political beliefs. (Jason Kempin)

O’Donnell said Judd was the one Trump supporter in her life she still maintained a friendship with, explaining that their bond had allowed them to put politics aside.

"I am friends with Wynonna Judd, who I love very much, and I’ve known her for many, many years. And she is a supporter of Trump. And somehow, we never bring it up," O’Donnell said.

O’Donnell went on to describe why she believed she could separate Judd’s alleged political views from their personal relationship.

Rosie O'Donnell said she believed longtime friend Wynonna Judd supported President Donald Trump. (Mike Marsland/Getty Images for Sky & NOW; Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)

"I kind of give her a grace in a way. She’s had so much in her life, with her mom taking her own life, and just the complicated nature of her upbringing. And I really love her and I care about her and for some reason I’m able to put that aside when we interact."

Her relationship with O’Donnell stretches back decades. Judd was a recurring guest on O’Donnell’s daytime talk show in the 1990s, and the pair have remained friends long after the program ended.

Meanwhile, O'Donnell has been an outspoken critic of Trump for years, with the comedian and president repeatedly trading public barbs.

After Trump won the 2024 presidential election, O’Donnell moved to Ireland with her child and has continued speaking publicly about American politics.
